articles.title: DOJ charges 28 with voting crimes. And, TikTok ignored staff's child safety concerns
articles.summary: The Justice Department has charged 28 people in California with voting crimes as Election Day nears. And, TikTok staff raised child safety concerns with executives, who failed to act, court records show.
body: Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

The Justice Department has charged 28 green card holders in California with election crimes for allegedly illegally registering to vote or voting in U.S. elections. This marks a significant escalation in the Trump administration's feud with the state over its voting system as the midterm elections approach. The DOJ also filed an emergency request to prevent California from processing ballots returned by people on the voter rolls that the federal government says are "likely noncitizens." California has sought clarification on the federal government's conclusions but has not received any. Last week, the DOJ sued California and Los Angeles County after local officials refused to investigate allegations made by the administration about noncitizen voting.

Democrats and Republicans are deciding which races to prioritize with Election Day just two weeks away. President Trump is campaigning in key perennial purple states like Georgia, North Carolina, Kansas, Iowa and Florida this week.

TikTok employees repeatedly raised concerns about the app's risks to children, including sexual exploitation and exposure to suicide content. Previously unreported court records show employees' frustration with leadership's response to these issues. Depositions filed in March 2026 provide new insights into TikTok's child safety measures since its surge in popularity in 2018. Staff alerted management about minors engaging with sexual content, which the company profited from. They also identified loopholes that allowed users under 18 to bypass age restrictions and block parental oversight of their app activity. The records show that TikTok avoided conducting age surveys, fearing it would have to share results with the Federal Trade Commission.

Cold and flu season in the U.S. starts this month and lasts through May, according ot the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Cooler temperatures and drier air can increase our vulnerability to illnesses like the common cold, flu, RSV and COVID-19. Get ahead of the game now by putting together a cold-and-flu prep kit. Here's what experts say you should have in your home.

For more advice on how to stock your medicine cabinet for cold and flu season, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.

Pleasant Rowland launched Pleasant Company in 1986 with three dolls — Samantha, Molly and Kirsten — creating an empire known as American Girl. To celebrate its 40th anniversary, author Fiona Davis was asked to write a historical fiction book for adults titled Samantha: The Next Chapter, featuring Samantha Parkington, who has turned 25. The story picks up after Samantha's last book, in which she attended a suffragist rally with her aunt Cornelia. The book is set 15 years later, in 1920, just after the ratification of the 19th Amendment. Samantha learns that her grandmother's inheritance has been stolen, forcing her to transition from socialite to shopgirl overnight. NPR's Samantha Balaban visited the American Girl store in New York with her own Samantha doll to explore the character's evolution over the years, drawing on insights from its staff and Davis. Check out photos from the visit and read more about the history of American Girl dolls.
This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

articles.title: Alberta voters reject a move toward independence in referendum backing Canadian unity
articles.summary: Voters in Canada's oil-rich province of Alberta have rejected a proposal to begin a process toward independence, results showed early Tuesday, delivering a victory for supporters of Canadian unity.
body: EDMONTON, Alberta — Voters in Canada's oil-rich province of Alberta have rejected a proposal to begin a process toward independence, results showed early Tuesday, delivering a victory for Prime Minister Mark Carney and supporters of Canadian unity amid U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war and annexation threats.
The vote was not a direct referendum on independence but would have set oil-rich Alberta on a path toward a future vote on separation from Canada.
With more than 1 million votes counted, about 76% supported remaining in Canada, compared with 23% who backed beginning a process that could lead to separation.
"We are a solid country that's united from coast to coast to coast," Thomas Lukaszuk, a former Alberta deputy premier who led the Forever Canadian campaign against separation, told supporters.

Results were delayed after late openings forced more than 100 polling stations to extend voting hours Monday. More than 1.35 million Albertans, or 43% of eligible voters, cast advance or special ballots. Albertans were deciding whether to remain in Canada or begin a legal process that could have lead to a second vote on separation.

Alberta, home to the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves, is cowboy country and a conservative stronghold whose political culture has long had more in common with the American West than much of Canada. Resentment toward Ottawa runs deep, but has not traditionally translated into widespread support for independence.
Dustin Degenhardt, a Wainwright voter, said Albertans have long been mistreated by Ottawa.
"Alberta has essentially been treated as, you know, a colony," he said after voting Monday. "They want to take and take and take from us and not return anything."
Taylor MacIsaac, another Wainwright voter, backed separation.
"I think it'll be good for Alberta to separate personally, as a very conservative individual that grew up in rural Alberta," she said.
Dave Malka, 59, of Edmonton, criticized spending money on a "referendum on a referendum" rather than health care.
With Trump threatening Canada, Malka said, "It seems to be happening at the absolute worst time when we should be united; instead we're fighting among ourselves."
Jake Graham, 35, of Calgary, attended a Carney rally wearing maple leaf pants and a Canada hockey jacket. He hopes the vote ends the debate.
"I hope this squashes this for a long time to come and that it's clear and decisive, that these grumblings disappear for a while and we can be a united Canada," he said.
Despite the proposal's apparent failure, separatist leaders have said they turned a fringe cause into a movement that will not disappear.
Carney earlier urged Albertans to deliver a decisive vote for unity. "Vote like Canada's future depends on it because it does," he told a rally Friday in Edmonton, where he grew up.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith called the referendum amid pressure from separatists within her governing United Conservative Party, even though she opposes independence. She cited a poll showing just 22% support for separation, a figure she said was still too high.

Separatist parties traditionally attracted only 1% or 2% of the vote, former Premier Jason Kenney said. Anger over COVID-19 restrictions helped mobilize activists who later embraced the separatist movement, he said.
Trump's trade war and threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state have helped Carney rally support in Alberta, where Liberal prime ministers have historically been unpopular.

Separatist advocate Jeff Rath said he would be thrilled if 30% of Albertans voted to begin the separation process. He wants Smith ousted as leader of her governing United Conservative Party and said the party could splinter, potentially creating a new pro-independence party.

articles.title: Australian prime minister says lawmaker critically injured by car is 'no accident'
articles.summary: A car hit an Australian federal independent lawmaker on Monday, critically injuring her in an apparent deliberate attack, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said. The driver was arrested.
body: MELBOURNE, Australia — A car hit an Australian federal independent lawmaker on Monday, critically injuring her in an apparent deliberate attack, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said. The driver was arrested.
Helen Haines, 65, was struck by a Toyota Land Cruiser SUV outside her electoral district office mid afternoon in the city of Wangaratta in Victoria state, a police said.
Albanese said the national counterterrorism team, incorporating police and intelligence agencies, was investigating.
"This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear. We don't know what the motivation is," Albanese told Australian Broadcasting Corp.
The 43-year-old driver was arrested at the scene by a passerby. He will be interviewed in relation to the incident, police said.
"A knife was located by police and seized from inside the Toyota," police said.
"At this stage, police are investigating as to whether this was an intentional act," police added.
Haines, who was first elected to the Parliament in 2019, was taken to a hospital with critical injuries, police said.

The episode has renewed safety concerns for Australian lawmakers, in a country where politicians have historically been highly accessible to the public and usually go about their business without security officers present. But public incitement against officials is growing.

Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett said in 2025 that threats against parliamentarians had doubled over the past three years. Police data showed more than 1,000 such threats against politicians in the 2025-2026 financial year, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Monday.
Albanese told the ABC it was "unfortunate" that an increasingly polarized political climate had already led to security changes for Australia's lawmakers.

"I think there has been a rise in temperature and there has been too much shouting, not enough discourse, not enough polite conversation and disagreement," he said Monday. There was "no question" that social media played a part, Albanese added.

In Britain, murders of politicians have prompted bolstered security. Labour lawmaker Jo Cox was shot and stabbed in 2016 by a far-right extremist, and Conservative David Amess was stabbed in 2021 by an attacker inspired by the Islamic State group.
In July, the former politician and reality TV contestant Ann Widdecombe was found slain with a hammer at her home. A man has been charged with murder and terrorism-related offenses.

articles.title: Alberta voters weigh future in Canada
articles.summary: On Monday voters in the oil-rich Canadian province of Alberta are deciding whether to take the first step toward a future referendum on independence.
body: EDMONTON, Alberta — For decades, Alberta separatism remained on the political margins. Now, voters in the oil-rich Canadian province are deciding whether to take the first step toward a future referendum on independence.

The nonbinding referendum vote on Monday is the first time the province has put the question of separation to a public vote, in what Elections Alberta has described as the largest electoral event in the province's history.
Polls indicate that Alberta voters will overwhelmingly reject the option of beginning the legal process toward a referendum on separation.

Pollsters generally estimate that about one in five Albertans support separation from Canada. But the vote has brought the question of Alberta's place in the Canadian federation to the forefront of public debate.
Essentially, this is a referendum about whether to hold another referendum on separation.

There are 10 questions in total. The first nine address immigration, access to provincial services such as health care, education and other social services, and potential changes to the Canadian Constitution. Voters can answer yes or no to each of these questions.

Question 10 offers voters two options. Option 1 asks whether Alberta should remain part of Canada, while option 2 asks whether the province should begin the legal process toward holding a referendum on separation.
Western alienation and grievances against Ottawa date back decades, including to the administrations of Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau, Justin Trudeau's father, during the 1970s and 1980s.
"I feel the Canadian system is broken. I know we aren't living in hell on earth. But it's the trajectory we're worried about and where things are going," says Cory Morgan.
Morgan founded the Alberta Independence Party in 2000 and is also the founder of Pathway to Independence, a third-party advertising group that advocates for an independent Alberta.

"Even if we don't get over the line on Monday, I would hope that some people understand that something large is brewing here and if we don't get some change, it's going to continue to grow," Morgan told NPR.

Support for separation intensified among some Albertans following COVID-19 lockdowns and vaccine mandates. Premier Danielle Smith said in May that it was "time to have a vote, understand the will of Albertans on this subject, and move on."
The referendum campaign brought Prime Minister Mark Carney back to his hometown of Edmonton on Friday, where he urged Albertans to keep their province in Canada ahead of the vote.
"A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and Canadians," Carney told the rally.

Alberta is one of Canada's wealthiest provinces and is home to the world's fourth-largest known oil reserves. The province contributes to Canada's equalization system, which provides federal funding to provinces with lower fiscal capacity. Some Albertans argue that the province should retain more of its revenue rather than see funds redistributed elsewhere in the country.
"We want to make a new country where we can stop sending our money 1,000 kilometers away in Ottawa," says Jeremy Clive, a 23-year-old pilot and university student from rural Alberta.
Leaving the Canadian federation would not be as simple as holding a referendum.

"It requires negotiating your way out," says Jared Wesley, a political scientist at the University of Alberta. "The Supreme Court has stated clearly that in order to leave, a province must negotiate with nine other provinces and the federal government to secure an amendment to the Constitution to remove themselves."
In 1995, Quebec held a referendum on sovereignty that narrowly rejected independence. The vote helped set the stage for Canada's Clarity Act, which Parliament passed in 2000.

The act states that secession negotiations can begin only after a referendum question and its result meet standards of clarity. It does not specify a fixed percentage that constitutes a clear majority. Any separation would also require constitutional negotiations involving provincial and federal governments.

"It's a bit ironic that separatists are a bit frustrated with the inability to change the constitution and they are using that as a pretext to leave, but, in order to leave, they need to change the same constitution with a much higher threshold for agreement," says Wesley.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has said she will respect the result and begin the process of holding a legally binding referendum, subject to the applicable legal requirements. That would not happen immediately.

The province would also need to consult with First Nations. Treaties between First Nations and the Crown predate Canadian Confederation, and First Nations groups have objected to the idea of an independent Alberta.

In May, an Alberta court ruled that a separatist petition seeking to trigger the referendum violated Indigenous rights because the province had failed to consult First Nations. The province has appealed the decision.

A government-commissioned report by the University of Calgary's School of Public Policy estimated that separating Alberta from Canada could cost as much as $170 billion Canadian dollars over five years. The report examined two scenarios involving a relatively smooth transition.

Under both scenarios, Alberta's debt would rise substantially as the province assumed a share of Canada's federal debt. The report projected that costs could range from $324 billion to $442.3 billion Canadian dollars.
An independent Alberta would also face billions of dollars in additional interest payments compared with what it currently pays as part of Canada.

Thomas Lukaszak, founder of Forever Canadian, a pro-unity movement, and a former deputy premier of Alberta, has spent 18 months campaigning across the province for Alberta to remain in Canada. He points to Quebec's 1995 referendum as a warning about the potential economic effects of separation.

"Several hundred thousand Canadians moved out of the province of Quebec and moved to other provinces," says Lukaszak. "And until today, the province of Quebec hasn't recovered economically from that because industry and investment has left Montreal and I'm fearing that the same thing would happen to the province of Alberta."

According to Elections Alberta, unofficial results for referendums with this many questions will be posted 48 hours after polls close. Recruiting enough staff for the vote has been a challenge, and Elections Alberta staff are expected to work around the clock to tally the results.
"This story won't end once the ballots are counted," says Wesley.
The referendum has highlighted deep divisions among Albertans. The question of separation is likely to remain prominent in the lead-up to the provincial election next year.

articles.title: Zelensky prepares for Oslo talks with US envoys as Rubio denies withholding intelligence
articles.summary: The US secretary of state rejects accusations Ukrainians were dying because the US was withholding intelligence.
body: Volodymyr Zelensky arrived at Oslo airport on Tuesday ahead of the talks with Witkoff
US special envoy Steve Witkoff has arrived in Norway ahead of talks with Volodymyr Zelensky with relations on the slide between the Ukrainian leader and US President Donald Trump.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said Zelensky had asked Oslo and neighbouring Finland to organise the meeting with the US and European allies "at a critical time for Ukraine".
Ahead of the meeting, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio rejected as "scandalous" and "outrageous" accusations that Ukrainians were dying because the US was withholding intelligence from Kyiv.
He was speaking after Zelensky's military technical adviser, Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, told the BBC that the lack of reliable US warnings meant lives were being lost.
"This looks very strange," said Beskrestnov. "Sometimes we receive this information before the attack, another time we [do] not."

Relations between Kyiv and the US have soured in recent weeks to the extent that Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".

Støre said the aim of the Oslo talks were to steer relations towards "a more constructive path". He told reporters at the parliament in Norway that they wanted to ensure that the war ended diplomatically with a lasting and just peace.
Zelensky said earlier he had had a "constructive discussion" with Rubio about the need for US early warnings, missile interceptors and SpaceX's Starlink internet network.

Last week a bipartisan group of US senators called for an urgent investigation into disruptions to the Starlink network in Ukraine, and unconfirmed reports on Tuesday said the transfer of more Patriot interceptors had not yet been approved.

The US secretary of state is currently on a visit to India and admitted to reporters that it may be true that Patriot interceptor missiles had not yet arrived in Ukraine, although nothing had been denied to Kyiv intentionally.
Steve Witkoff was due to hold talks in Oslo in person while Jared Kushner was taking part remotely

Witkoff is expected to be joined by video-link by Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, and by several European representatives, including Finnish President Alexander Stubb and officials from the UK, Poland, France and Germany, as well as the EU and Nato.

It is not yet clear whether Witkoff will travel on to Russia after his visit to Oslo, however the Kremlin spokesman said he hoped a meeting with Trump's special envoy could be organised in the near future. Dmitry Peskov said "we greatly appreciate the mediation efforts of the American negotiators".

Earlier this month Russia's Vladimir Putin discussed the war with Trump over the phone, and not long afterwards the US president announced that Moscow would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the US and other markets, bringing to an end American sanctions on Russian diesel exports.

European leaders have expressed concern about recent statements from the US towards Russia, and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz spoke on Monday of "mixed pictures and messages" on the war, adding that he was trying to convince the American government "in total that this is something we have to resolve jointly".
He pointed out that the US had not been paying for the defence of Ukraine since the start of 2025, and Europe and other countries were shouldering the burden.

"It's really a big effort for our budgets, it's really a big thing for the European Union, but we are doing that and we are trying to keep on doing that until this terrible war ends," the German leader told Bloomberg TV.

Asked whether or not Ukraine was a US ally, Vice-President JD Vance has said in a TV interview that Kyiv was "certainly a partner in some ways, but we have some divergent interests from time to time, like for example... I think they should stop bombing Russian energy".

"We don't have a formal alliance as far as I know with Ukraine. They're not in Nato, I don't think they should be in Nato... we're gonna work together on some things, but also we're going to be opposite on some things too."

articles.title: Man charged with attack on Australian MP as suspect's father says she is family friend
articles.summary: Brendan Nugent's family say they have known Helen Haines, who remains in a critical condition, for more than 20 years.
body: The community in Wangaratta remains in shock after the alleged attack
A 43-year-old man has been charged after Australian MP Helen Haines was hit by a car in Victoria state on Monday.

The suspect will appear in court on Wednesday to face charges of dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a public official.

Local media earlier named the alleged attacker as environmental activist Brendan Nugent. His father and his partner said they had been friends with Haines "for more than 20 years" and thanked residents and officers who helped her after the "shocking and horrific crime".
Haines remains in a critical condition after surgery and is reported to have lost one of her legs.
"Helen Haines is a deeply respected, valued and much loved member of our local community," Rod Nugent and his partner Christine Cunningham said in a statement.
"All of our love and all of our thoughts are with Helen and her family and friends."
They promised to assist Victoria Police "in any way we can".
Police say they will allege the incident was targeted.
Haines, 65, the independent member for Indi, is in a critical but stable condition after undergoing surgery at a Melbourne hospital.
'Our worst nightmare': Threats to Australian politicians were rising before MP hit by car
Shock and disbelief: How the attack on an Australian MP unfolded
What we know about Australian MP hit by car in apparent deliberate attack
She was airlifted there after bystanders rushed to help as the suspect allegedly struck her twice outside her office in Wangaratta.
The driver reportedly did a U-turn to get into position before hitting her, then reversed and hit her again, the home affairs minister told national broadcaster ABC.
She was pinned between two cars and later lost a leg, the ABC reports. The outlet also says doctors are fighting to save her other leg.
A local barber says he pulled the suspect out of his car and took a knife from him.
"I just wasn't comfortable with his movements so I took it out of his pocket and threw it away," Ricky Jefferies told reporters.
"I don't think I'm a hero. I think that I was just a person who had an opportunity to intervene in a safe-ish way."
Others who helped "didn't even check for danger," Jefferies said. "The car was still on and they sat in front of a rolling car, that's not an exaggeration."
Ricky Jefferies describes how he pulled the suspect out of the car
In their statement, Victoria Police say a highway patrol unit was nearby at the time of the incident and "on scene" within eight seconds of the call coming through.
As they announced the charges against the 43-year-old, they said they had searched a property in Tarrawingee, around 12km (7.5 miles) from Wangaratta.
"At this stage it appears this is an isolated incident, and there are currently no other known threats connected to this matter," they said, adding officers would maintain a presence in Wangaratta.
Haines won the seat of Indi as an independent in 2019, and has since become a prominent member of the crossbench, building rapport across Australia's increasingly divided political spectrum.
The community, and country, remain in shock.
At a vigil on Tuesday, locals queued patiently in the cathedral aisle, waiting for their turn to light a candle. Priests hugged some of those who came to pay their respects.
Wangaratta's main street, where Haines's office is located, had reopened to traffic. Cars slowly filed past the growing number of bouquets being left for her on the pavement.
One card read: "May you recover quickly and continue to be a light in this world."

articles.title: Suspect arrested after historic town hall set alight - French media
articles.summary: The spire of the clock tower at Limoges city hall dramatically collapsed as it was engulfed in flames on Saturday.
body: A suspect linked to a far-left movement has been arrested in France after a 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire over the weekend that broke out during mass disorder, French media reports.
The clock tower and parts of the roof of the ornate city hall in the central city of Limoges were engulfed in flames before collapsing on Saturday.
The 34-year-old suspect is known to police for acts of violence against public officials and is on the "S" list, a French national security watchlist, FranceInfo and BFMTV reported.
Meanwhile in Marseille, a curfew for young people will be introduced on Tuesday evening.
The city's mayor Benoît Payan said that the prefect had decided to introduce the curfew in Marseille "starting this evening and for days to come".
He said the measures apply to minors and will only be in commercial areas of the city, which were particularly affected by looting which took place last weekend.
More than 120 people have already been imprisoned following widespread demonstrations over the weekend, French Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin told CNews-Europe.
Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets to protest against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.
Darmanin said he asked prosecutors to be "extremely firm" and "ruthless towards those who attacked police officers, gendarmes and firefighters, who looted shops and who attacked public buildings".
The justice minister insisted France did not need to be put into a state of emergency which would "deprive all French people of their individual freedoms".
But French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu earlier said he had not ruled out imposing a state of emergency.
The city hall's roof and clock tower in Limoges was severely damaged in the fire
Targeted curfews introduced across France on Monday contributed to a quiet night following the disorder, Lecornu said.
Curfews were introduced across parts of central Paris, including Place de la République, where protesters had gathered over the weekend, and the Les Halles shopping area.

Other measures restricting the movement of young people and gatherings were introduced on Monday in cities such as Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south, as well as Lille and other towns in the north.
Lecornu thanked police officers and gendarmes for enforcing the measures, adding that further curfews on Tuesday night would be decided depending on where they were necessary.
Writing in a post on X, he said decisions would be made "on the ground" by French regions and local mayors.
The streets in the southern city of Lyon were quiet on Monday night
Earlier Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez admitted police had "lost control" in some cities.
He was strongly criticised by opposition politicians over authorities' preparedness for the disorder, leading him to offer his resignation on Monday, which was rejected by President Emmanuel Macron.

More than 2,500 people have been arrested since the disorder broke out, officials said on Monday. One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to the AFP news agency. About 1,000 police officers were injured.

Protests first began last month with students demanding better school conditions but they have escalated to take in a broader range of concerns with numbers at demonstrations bolstered by trade unions and various protest groups.
Riots took place across French cities, including the capital Paris
More than 2,000 shops and other businesses have been directly impacted by the weekend's violence, the head of France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI) said.
Rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, were seen setting fire to cars and buildings and looting businesses in Paris, Marseille and other cities and smaller towns.
Protest organisers have declared that a second round of protests will take place on Saturday across France.
The so-called yellow vests (gilets jaunes), who were responsible for France's longest-ever modern protests in 2018, has said "Act II" will take place this weekend.
Meanwhile, French union La CGT has called for a major day of strikes on 5 November.

articles.title: Seventh day of violent clashes between Albanian protesters and police
articles.summary: Almost 300 people have been injured, more than half of them police, as violent anti-government demonstrations show no sign of easing.
body: Protesters in Albania have fought with riot police on the seventh consecutive day of violent clashes.

The protesters, many of them high school and university students, are trying to oust embattled Prime Minister Edi Rama. Official figures said 295 people have been injured, 186 of whom are police officers, before Monday's violence.
"The moment the state negotiates with this," Rama told grim-faced police chiefs, brandishing a rock hurled at police on Sunday, "the state has fallen".

A police station and government buildings in Tirana have been attacked during the protests, which are being driven by demands for better university conditions, anger over corruption and calls for Rama's resignation.
The protesters included "young men and women who have been radicalised by dark forces in Europe and the US", Rama said. "Albania has become one of the targets of a well co-ordinated attack."

In brilliant October sunshine in Rinia Park, also known as Youth Park, I watched people prising loose cobble stones - like that brandished by the prime minister - as ammunition for later battles with police. They did not have long to wait.
People in Rinia park loosen cobblestones to use as ammunition against riot police
A convoy of police vehicles advanced down a broad boulevard, led by an armoured truck firing water cannon and tear gas canisters among the fleeing protesters.
Squads of riot police chased the predominantly student crowd through the park. Protesters took refuge in a cafe where even the eyes of the waiters streamed from the teargas.

Under trees, volunteers in yellow reflector jackets stood their ground helping those overcome by the fumes. I watched a young man remonstrating with a policeman, who then fired pepper spray in his face at point-blank range.
"The police actions are often chaotic and stupid," human rights lawyer Gentian Sejrani told the BBC. He provides legal support to more than 100 people who have been arrested.
"In court, the police rarely present evidence," he said. His clients include a man arrested on his way to a bus stop – completely unrelated to the protests, he said.
"Those who are actually throwing stuff at the police rarely get caught, because they run the fastest," Serjani said.
Police appear as incensed by the violence against their colleagues as the protesters are by the strong-arm tactics of the police. The result is mayhem.
Protesters were ready with saline spray to help to relieve the effects of tear gas

Outside the cafe in the park, when the gas has cleared, 27-year-old activist Sidorela Vatnikaj, a masters student, describes her typical day. In a movement without leaders she is one of the more experienced, with eight years in the forefront of anti-government protests behind her.

"In the morning, you try to co-ordinate with all the groups - where they are, and where the protest is taking place. If any lawyers are needed, if any first aid kit or any kind of equipment is needed. And you also have to make sure all your friends, your family members in the protest are OK."
The day is spent going from protest to protest, much of it running from police, she said.
She is uncomfortable with the violence towards the authorities from her fellow protesters, but blames the police for starting and fuelling it.
"When I see people throwing stones at the police, I understand their anger. I don't judge them. I'm not happy, but they have no other way to be listened to," Vatnikaj said.

"They come from families whose family members had no other choice than to leave the country - a million in the past decade. They have not only been robbed, they have been bullied, ignored and now they they have also been beaten up."
At the weekend, the prime minister asked rhetorically what would happen if he stepped down.

"We need a technocratic government for one year, to prepare the country for real, democratic elections," Vatnikaj replies. She has accused Rama of rigging previous elections, and of being hand in glove with rich foreign investors and organised crime groups.
Young people in Albania feel encouraged by their fellow Gen Z protesters around the world, Vatnikaj said.
"I have seen my mother and father's generation, working all their lives and dreaming of having a democratic society where they could live with dignity. That never happened," she said.

Rama has been in power for 13 years, and has been a dominant figure in Albanian politics since the turn of the century. He has promised EU membership by 2030, and said he is the only one who can deliver it.

articles.title: Canadian tourist found guilty of animal cruelty after stealing Las Vegas flamingo from enclosure
articles.summary: The man testified that he snatched Peachy from its enclosure at the Flamingo hotel and casino after drinking 30 to 40 beers, but did not mean any harm.
body: Fairbarn was seen on CCTV in an elevator on the way to his hotel room with the flamingo
A Canadian man has been found guilty of animal cruelty after he took a flamingo from its enclosure in Las Vegas and brought it back to his hotel room during an alcohol-fuelled bender.
Mitchell Fairbarn, who was visiting the US city, took the Chilean flamingo named Peachy from the Flamingo Las Vegas Hotel and Casino in March.

Videos shown at his trial showed a smiling Fairbarn carrying the bird by the neck as he took a lift to his room. He testified that he had drunk 30 to 40 beers before the incident and said he never meant to harm the animal. He faces nearly five years in prison.
Animal experts testified the flamingo had feathers torn out and suffered blood loss due to Fairbarn's actions.
A lawyer for Fairbarn said his actions were intended as a harmless prank, and blamed alcohol for his "bad decisions".
"He should not have done that, should not have gone into the habitat, shouldn't have touched a bird, shouldn't have taken Peachy inside," said his lawyer Josh Tomsheck, external.
"The truth is, Mitch was drunk. Mitch was stupid. He made bad decisions."
His lawyer added he had received death threats since his arrest.
Testifying in his defence, Fairbarn, 34, said he thought it would be "funny" to take the bird.
He said he had been up drinking all night and had just gotten off a call with a colleague when he made the decision to abscond with the bird.

The Flamingo Las Vegas, located along the famous Las Vegas strip, features a wildlife habitat inside its hotel and casino that is free to walk through. It features a flock of Chilean flamingos, other birds, fish and turtles.
During the trial, the jury heard from 14 witnesses and reviewed more than 112 pieces of evidence, according to CBS, the BBC's US partner.
It took a jury around five hours to convict him on felony and misdemeanour animal abuse charges.
Fairbarn has been unable to leave the US since his arrest. He remains on house arrest in Las Vegas, with a sentencing hearing due to take place in December.
A veterinarian for the state said that Peachy has largely recovered since the event but has a now has a more anxious demeanour around humans.

articles.title: Why Israeli Gen Z voters are drawn to the far right
articles.summary: More than half a million young people will cast their ballots in Israel next week - and they could make all the difference.
body: Far-right minister Ben Gvir (left) has significant support among Israeli youth
When Israel's far-right National Security Minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, reached voting age, he was rejected from Israel's army for being too politically extreme.
His views have not changed much in the 30 years since then - but Israel has. Once shunned by the political establishment, he is now part of the government's inner sanctum of ministers.

On the campaign trail ahead of Israel's general elections next week, Ben Gvir is often surrounded by a jubilant pack of fresh-faced young fans, waving huge party flags over the heads of his numerous security guards.
At the covered market in Ramle - a mixed city of Jewish and Arab Israelis - he told us his message to young voters was to get out and vote.
"We see the support, we see the love [and] we want to win!" he said.
Nadav, 18, believes Ben Gvir is "trying to show that Israel is a strong country"
More than half a million first-time voters will cast their ballots in this election, which many Israelis see as existential for Israel's future security and identity.
Polls suggest it will be a tight race, and the new young voters could help decide the result.

More than 16% are planning to support far-right parties - either Ben Gvir's Jewish Power or the Religious Zionism party of his far-right ally Bezalel Smotrich - according to a poll for one of Israel's most popular newspapers, Yedioth Ahronoth.
And almost three-quarters see themselves as "right or centre-right", according to another survey for Israel's leading Channel 12 television network.
"Itamar Ben Gvir gives me a sense of security," said 20-year-old Mordechai, one of the young fans accompanying the politician to Ramle.
"Like everyone in history, from Trump to Moses, there are slips of the tongue that are a bit less good. So what? 90% of the things by Itamar are amazing."
"Itamar will give us safety, and when we go to the army, someone will have our backs and be behind us," said 18-year-old Nadav.
"I think he's trying to show that we're a strong country. For many years, we couldn't show we're strong in our beliefs. We couldn't express our ideology."

Meir Schreiber, an ultra-Orthodox 23-year-old who grew up in London, said the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks on Israel, which triggered the Gaza war, also convinced him that Ben Gvir was the right choice.
"Young people understand that peace isn't something we can do," he told me, "because what happens to you when you're young shapes your personality - we saw October 7."
Polls suggest more than 16% of first-time voters are planning to support far-right parties next week

Ben Gvir is a divisive candidate in a divided nation: his political positions include annexation of the occupied West Bank, Jewish settlement of Gaza, and the "voluntary emigration" of Palestinians - positions and rhetoric that are widely condemned by liberal Israelis.

Several Western countries have imposed sanctions or travel bans on Ben Gvir and Smotrich for incitement against Palestinians. Both men are powerful ministers in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's governing coalition.
As he and his entourage pushed their way between the stalls, some shopkeepers threw sweets; others, dark looks.
"I don't like him, he sows discord," one stallholder said. "Ramle is a mixed city - Jews and Arabs. There's no problem here, even after 7 October, but his message preys on young uneducated people."
The fact that he appears more popular with 18 to 22-year-olds than with their parents' generation is often put down, at least partly, to the impact of the 7 October attacks.
But political analyst Dahlia Scheindlin, who previously ran many Israeli political campaigns, said it was more than that.
"For about the last 20 years, we've seen young Israeli Jews are more right wing than average, and significantly more right-wing on many measures than the 55+ group," she told me.

"They have grown up under a series of wars with no personal experience of efforts to achieve peace. But for the most part, they have been socialised into the most extreme terms of the debate [as] legitimate to discuss: annexation, settlement expansion and - after 7 October - annexation of Gaza. And now they're voting for the first time."
Mordechai, 20, says Ben Gvir's "slips of the tongue" do not matter
A series of classroom debates filmed by Israeli satirist Lior Schleien recently highlighted the extreme views of some young Israelis.

The debates, in which he challenges racist or extreme views, drew a lot of attention in Israel, and included one exchange in which a student advocates killing all Arab citizens of Israel. That particular video has since been removed from Schleien's website.

Surveys suggest that first-time voters here are highly motivated to cast their ballots, with more than 80% saying they are likely to do so. But the same research suggests they are also more sceptical about democratic institutions and less engaged by political protests or petitions.
In a race that is largely deadlocked between two stable blocs of pro-government and anti-government supporters, getting new voters to the polling stations could make all the difference.
Opposition parties have been engaging younger voters with warnings about threats to democracy, new social media videos and younger candidates.
Polls show Benjamin Netanyahu and his coalition allies in a tight race with the opposition bloc

"In 2022 [in the last election], only 59% of the citizens living in Tel Aviv voted - in the most liberal city in the whole Middle East! In places where they voted for Ben Gvir, they voted at around 90%," said Yonatan Shalev, a 24-year-old candidate with the centre-right opposition party, Beyachad ("Together"), led by former prime minister Naftali Bennett.
He told me that Ben Gvir had understood the power of social media faster than other politicians.
"The liberal politicians didn't believe in TikTok, didn't believe in Instagram, and he took advantage of that arena."
Shalev said he had pushed his own party to reach young voters through social media.

"Three months ago, Ben Gvir was still the politician with the most amount of views on TikToks, the most amount of likes on TikTok, and Instagram as well," he explained. "Right now, Naftali Bennett is leading [that]."

His boss's Instagram page now features videos of the former prime minister lifting weights to rap music, or chatting with Shalev in the street. Even Netanyahu has joined in with a fast-paced militaristic social media video set to heavy beats.
"Younger people don't watch the news in Israel, [they] don't read the newspapers. The younger generation is getting all its details from TikTok and Instagram".
Beyachad candidate Yonatan Shalev says Ben Gvir understood social media's power sooner than others
Yahlee Reske and Mika Magal, both 21 years old, rushed out of a nearby bar when they saw Shalev walk past.
"Yes," agreed Yahlee. "He's our age, he's so young and knows so much. It's hard to listen to people who are old and saying the same things over and over again."
Yahlee said she was doing national military service when the 7 October attacks unfolded.
"I don't think I ever looked at politics until then," she said. "But maybe if the government had been different on 7 October, things would have been better."

The same poll suggesting 16% of first-time voters would back a far-right party also suggested that Beyachad alone would take almost 9% of their votes, as would the centre-right Yashar party of Gadi Eisenkot.
At a student event in Tel Aviv last weekend, Ben Gvir was interrupted by protesters shouting, "Fascism will not pass", and forced off the stage.

Israel's young voters may be moving to the right, but they are still as divided as their country, over who they believe is the guardian of Israel's security and identity, and who is an existential threat.

articles.title: Residents warned not to drink tap water after hundreds fall sick near South Africa capital
articles.summary: More than 400 people, mostly children, become ill after drinking contaminated water, east of Pretoria.
body: Tests found traces of E. coli in water supplied to residents living near Pretoria

Residents living near South Africa's capital, Pretoria, have been warned not to drink or cook with tap water after more than 400 people, mostly children under four, fell ill after drinking contaminated water.
The cases were detected in Tshwane, the area which includes Pretoria, after people reported to their local hospital with "stomach cramps and diarrhoea" over a two-week period, officials said.
No deaths have been reported but high levels of E. coli were found in the water.
Tshwane has faced numerous outbreaks from waterborne diseases in recent years. In 2023, 29 people were killed by a cholera outbreak in a township just outside Pretoria.
That outbreak, in Hammanskraal, was linked to substandard water purification practices.
In 2025, officials confirmed 48 cases of typhoid in the same area east of Pretoria. The source of the outbreak remains unclear.
No cholera bacteria has been found in the latest cases.
The departments of water and health, in a joint statement on Monday, said 408 cases had been detected between 7 and 18 October in about five townships.

They said that lab tests "indicate that the illness has been caused by residents being exposed to contaminated water" from a local water treatment facility supplying water to several communities east of Pretoria.
Samples tested found norovirus, campylobacter, shigella and "other pathogens that cause stomach cramps and diarrhoea", officials said.
The team's early investigations found that local authorities had failed to warn residents about the contaminated water.

The water supplied to the area has been declared unfit for human consumption and authorities urged residents to only use it to flush toilets. Tankers have been dispatched to supply clean drinking water.
"Previously stored water should be discarded, and water containers must be disinfected using household bleach," officials said.

articles.title: Mission blasts off for Mars to grab a piece of its moon
articles.summary: A spacecraft is set to launch on an ambitious mission to bring 10g of Martian moon dust back to Earth.
body: Watch: Spacecraft heading to Mars' moon Phobos lifts off from Japan
A spacecraft has launched from Japan headed for Mars' moon Phobos, where it will attempt to grab some moondust and bring it back to Earth.
If it is successful, this will become the first time a sample has been returned from Mars or its moons to be analysed in laboratories here on Earth.
The spacecraft is scheduled to arrive at Phobos in August 2027.
It is hoped that the Mars Moons Exploration (MMX) mission, which is led by the Japanese Space Agency, will solve the mystery of how Mars's moons formed.

Prof Sara Russell, from the Natural History Museum, who is the MMX mission's deputy for sample analysis, said: "There hasn't yet been a successful mission to go to Phobos and bring a bit back to Earth.
"I think this is an incredibly ambitious and fun mission," she said.
There are only three moons in the inner Solar System: our own Moon, and two around Mars, which are called Phobos and Deimos.
Both of these are tiny - Phobos is about 20km (12 miles) across and Deimos is about 10km (six miles) across. They are also irregularly shaped, looking a bit like space potatoes.
The MMX spacecraft will study Deimos as it arrives in the Mars neighbourhood, and then will focus on Phobos.
It plans to set down a small rover to explore the terrain, though this will be no easy feat.
Sara Russell says no one has ever landed a rover on such a small moon.
"The moon itself doesn't have very much of its own gravity," she explained.
"But it's next to an enormous planet that's got a much higher gravity, and that makes it much harder to get a rover onto the surface."
Mars got its moons about 4.5bn years ago - but no one knows how they formed
The rover will scout out a landing site so that the MMX spacecraft itself can later touch down on Phobos.
Once on the surface, it will deploy a robotic arm and two samplers to grab some moon dust.
This material will be packed into a small capsule that will return to Earth in 2031, landing in the Woomera desert of South Australia.
The amount of material that will come back is tiny - just 10g.
"It's a very small [amount] actually," said Dr Chrysa Avdellidou, from Leicester University, who is working with the Japanese mission.
"However we can do several studies even on individual grains… You don't need to have kilos back from a surface in order to do science. So it's worth every gram," she said.
The spacecraft will collect 10g of moon dust from the surface of Phobos
Scientists believe the sample will finally shed light on the puzzle of where Mars's moons came from.
Either a space rock smashed into Mars early in its history, and Phobos and Deimos were created from the debris.
Or the moons are two wandering asteroids from the outer Solar System, which were grabbed by the Red Planet's gravity.
"When we get the sample back, we'll be able to look in detail at its chemistry and its mineral composition - and the two hypotheses will produce very distinct results," said Sara Russell.
"It should be pretty much immediately obvious.. whether it's the product of this dramatic impact or whether it's a captured asteroid. So we'll find that out really quickly."
The team is also hoping there might be an extra bonus coming back to their labs.

"One of the really exciting things is that Phobos is so close to the Mars surface that whenever there's an impact into the Mars surface, little grains might actually become implanted into Phobos itself," said Russell.
"And that means that the sample we get back may actually contain grains of Mars as well. So it can give us really direct information about the composition and history of Mars."
Martian meteorites are rare - this one is on display at the Natural History Museum
Bringing material from Mars back to Earth has long been an ambition of space scientists.
The Nasa Perseverance rover, which has been exploring Mars since 2021, has been carefully collecting samples on Mars and storing them in canisters.
But a second Nasa/ESA mission, called Mars Sample Return, that would have picked up and returned these canisters, has been effectively cancelled, after its funding was halted by the US Congress.
China is planning its own sampling mission to Mars, set to launch in 2028. It will attempt to return Martian material to Earth in 2031.
We do already have some fragments of the Red Planet here on Earth in the form of Martian meteorites.
These are pieces of Mars that were blasted off the surface by asteroid strikes, and ended up being hurled towards the Earth.
Martian meteorites are extremely rare, but like all space rocks that fall to our planet, they become contaminated as soon as they get here, mixing with the air, dust, soil and water.
Scientists are so desperate to get their gloved hands on a direct sample from Mars and its moons because it would be pristine.

articles.title: Kenya pastor accused of ordering parents to starve their children to death faces verdict
articles.summary: Prosecutors say Paul Mackenzie lured the latest victims to their deaths by writing notes from his prison cell.
body: Paul Mackenzie operated his church for 16 years, attracting thousands of followers
A Kenyan court is set to deliver a judgement in a mass murder case involving doomsday preacher Paul Mackenzie.
Mackenzie and 29 of his followers are being charged with the murder of 191 children.
His cult is alleged to have forced children to starve to death so that they could "meet Jesus". His doomsday doctrine said that education was forbidden and modern medicine was considered "evil".
Mackenzie and the 29 others have all pleaded not guilty to murder, repeatedly insisting that nobody was forced to die.
Mackenzie's former head of security, Enos Amanya Ngala, was initially accused but then entered a plea deal and became a witness for the prosecution.
Mackenzie and other leaders of the cult are facing a raft of other legal cases, including for terrorism, radicalisation and denying education to children.
But this is the first time the pastor will face a verdict on the most serious charges of murder.
Authorities said over 400 bodies were found in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast, where Mackenzie led his followers from across the country.
Seventeen men were hired from the nearby town for the horrifying task of digging up the shallow graves. Some were paid just $8 (£6) a day.
"Every grave we found had at least three bodies," James, one of the gravediggers, told the BBC. "Some of the remains were of children as young as a few weeks old."
"We once found 12 bodies of children in a line inside a grave. It was massive, the bodies were arranged like clothes. One on top of another."
Gravediggers described some of the bodies of children as having had their "hands and legs tied and bodies wrapped in bedsheets".
Salim Karisa was paid about $8 a day to dig up dozens of bodies

Although many of Mackenzie's followers were from elsewhere in Kenya, some of the remains are of people who were familiar to the community because the people in the cult would often go to nearby Shakahola town for supplies and to fetch water from the River Galana which flows through the town.
"We would sometimes carry people on our motorbikes into the forest," said Salim Karisa, another gravedigger. "But it was so planned and secretive that nobody could tell what was happening inside."

Stephen Mwiti, 48, recounted losing all six of his children to the cult and seeing "many bald women and tens of children" surrounding Mackenzie in his house when he went to confront him. Mackenzie forbade make-up and hairstyles, so told women to shave off their hair or keep it unkempt.
Mwiti's former wife is one of those accused alongside Mackenzie.
"If I met Pastor Mackenzie today, one of us will have to die," told the BBC.
Stephen Mwiti says his six children died in the forest
"All six of my children died in Shakahola forest," Mwiti said, visibly emotional holding a photograph of his family. "I only found and buried the remains of my son Samuel."

"This little thing here was the start of all my misery," Mwiti said as he pointed at a dusty TV and cable box in his home in the coastal town of Malindi, 70km (43 miles) from Shakahola. It was from that TV that Mackenzie's doctrine made it to his home.
The pastor established Good News International Ministries in 2003. Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity to draw thousands of followers in the church's branches across Kenya.
His church ran a television station called Times TV which would broadcast his sermons from his church in Malindi.
His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil".
This is the building from where Mackenzie broadcast his sermons
Mackenzie's son, Dan Paul Mackenzie, said he worked as a cameraperson in the church. "The children would sit at the back, adults in the middle, and everyone would sing worship songs all morning."
The pastor would start his fiery sermons at noon, some of which included "casting out demons".
The main church shut down in 2019 and Paul Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him.

Peter Shukrani, 23, says his mother relocated to Shakahola with him at the time. He started going to Mackenzie's church when he was eight years old and described him as his "spiritual father", adding that he would "never say a bad word about him".
When in the forest, Shukrani fell ill and his condition deteriorated because medication was banned.
"My mother would throw away all the medicine I was supposed to take because she believe that only God could heal me," Shukrani said.
The community was described as mud houses scattered across the vast forest. "We lived a quiet normal life, fasting for a few days then having a small meal," Shukrani said.

By March 2023 when the first remains were discovered by local herders, hundreds of people had died. "We would carry someone out of the forest but they were so frail that they would die in our arms," explained Salim Karisa, one of the gravediggers.
Shukrani was one of the men rescued from the forest in March 2023.
He was ill and bed-ridden for weeks until that point, but his condition worsened because his mother would throw away all the medication he needed to recover.
"My mother believed Pastor Mackenzie's doctrine that medicine was evil," Shukrani said.
"I would have died if I wasn't rescued from Shakahola forest."
Peter Shukrani says he would have died if he had stayed in the forest but still believes Mackenzie is a good man
In the 298 pages detailing the charges against him in the current case, all of the 191 victims Mackenzie and his followers are accused of murdering are children.
Many of the bodies are still unidentified, owing to their advanced state of decomposition.
In the court documents, several are referred to as "unknown male child" and identified by the location of their grave and date of their discovery.

Despite the suffering endured by Mackenzie's followers, men, women and children who died due to starvation, strangulation and even being bludgeoned to death, as well as his own suffering, Shukrani believes Mackenzie was "a good person who cares for me".
"Mackenzie didn't force anyone to fast. People made those choices by themselves because of their beliefs," Shukrani said.
"I still love him and he is still my pastor."
In contrast Dan Mackenzie believes his father should be found guilty of murder.
"He was the leader, he was someone who they were looking [up to]. So he is a murderer of mass killing."

articles.title: Tennis star Svitolina says emotional toll of Ukraine war led to Monfils separation
articles.summary: The two top tennis pros married in 2021 and have one child together.
body: Monfils and Svitolina played in the mixed doubles together at this year's US Open and reached the semi-finals
Ukrainian tennis star Elina Svitolina has announced the end of her marriage with French former tennis player Gaël Monfils, citing the emotional impact of the war in her country.
The 32-year-old, who is ranked number six in the world, wrote in a heartfelt post on Instagram about the effect the conflict and "what the war has done to me inside".
"This is the most difficult thing I have ever had to share," she wrote, saying "I need to find my way back to myself". Svitolina said she felt she could not do that within her marriage.
She said her husband Monfils, 40, "listened" and "respected what I need with a strength and grace I will never forget".
"Some battles happen deep inside you, and no amount of love from someone else can win them for you," the four-time Grand Slam semi-finalist wrote.
It was "the hardest thing I have ever had to tell the person I love", Svitolina said.
"Everyone knows how much Ukraine means to me," Svitolina, who grew up in Odesa, said.
Ukraine's Black Sea port city has been heavily bombed by Russia throughout the war.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
"What you didn't see were the sleepless nights, the doubts, and the feeling of slowly losing myself."
The tennis power couple married in 2021 and have one child together - a four-year-old daughter called Skai.
Svitolina said her daughter "will always come first", adding "our marriage is ending, but our family is not".
Monfils, a former world number six, was expected to play the final tournament of his career at next month's Paris Masters in an emotional farewell.
However, the two-time Grand Slam semi-finalist's retirement was effectively confirmed last week when he appeared on the International Tennis Integrity Authority's list of retired players.
Once a player removes themselves from anti-doping protocols, they are not eligible to compete in professional tournaments.
Monfils, who won 13 titles on the ATP Tour, is preparing to start a new career in finance after joining a Swiss wealth management firm.

articles.title: Vinted blocks French looters listing stolen goods for sale
articles.summary: The platform said since the weekend it had "taken immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to looting".
body: Vinted says it has removed listings of items believed to have been looted from shops during the ongoing riots in France.
The second hand re-selling platform said following the weekend's disorder it had "taken immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to looting".
Shops across several French cities were broken into and ransacked during the outbreak of riots over the weekend.
"The sale of stolen goods, or soliciting them, is strictly prohibited on Vinted, and we have zero tolerance for it," a spokesperson for the company said.

Widespread looting was reported across Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas after protests against the cost of living and public spending turned into riots, leading to the arrests of at least 1,200 people.
More than 2,000 businesses were directly impacted by the weekend's violence, according to the head of the Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI).
Alain Di Crescenzo told France's broadcaster RTL that the riots led to hundreds of millions of euros worth of damage.
Groups of rioters, some wearing masks and balaclavas, were seen setting fire to cars and buildings as well as looting businesses.
Those that stole goods now appear to be looking to sell them on fast.
"Since this weekend, our teams have taken immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to the looting, and we have stepped up monitoring of suspicious listings," Vinted told the BBC.
"When our rules are breached, we act against the accounts involved, up to permanent bans."
France is one of Vinted's largest markets, along with the UK and Italy.
The company said it was working with French authorities and the police, and was adapting its "processes to detect and counter emerging risks and malicious behaviour".

eBay has not noted any increase in listings linked to the looting in France, but said it works with law enforcement to investigate suspected stolen goods and takes appropriate action, including removing listings and taking action against sellers, when authorities confirm an item is stolen.
French PM calls for partial curfews as he condemns 'thieves' and 'thugs' behind riots
Reuters news agency reported luxury shops and boutiques were shuttered and surrounded by security guards at the Place Vendome in Paris.
But it said a host of stores in the French capital, including Dior, Rolex, Louis Vuitton and Ralph Lauren had their shopfronts damaged
In Marseille, football club Olympique de Marseille said its official store on the city's historic main avenue had been looted.
It has closed the store, along with fellow Ligue 1 club Lille, which said its club shop would remain closed until further notice.

articles.title: Ex-OpenAI worker accused of planting device had Saudi support says court filing
articles.summary: The Saudi government did not immediately respond to BBC requests for comment.
body: A Saudi national charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's meeting rooms has been accused of having "considerable support" from the Saudi government, according to a court filing, external in California.

US prosecutors claimed Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked for the AI firm, was in "frequent communication... with a member of the Saudi royal family", and say a member of the country's military paid for a one-way flight to Saudi Arabia for his wife and son after his arrest.
It was argued the 35-year-old engineer therefore posed a flight risk and should be detained, pending trial.
The Saudi government did not immediately respond to BBC requests for comment.
Alfozan had worked at OpenAI for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant an audio recorder.
The AI company discovered the device, which was plugged into the back of a TV in a conference meeting room and covered up with toilet paper, on 30 September.
A camera was placed in the room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering and appearing to look behind the television where the audio recorder had been inserted.
He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI was terminated.

The court filing claimed the suspect's alleged conduct could pose "a danger to the national security of the United States", because executives from the tech firm met with government officials in the room during the days the device was believed to have been installed.
It said Alfozan's arrest came three days before he was scheduled to fly from San Francisco to Riyadh on a one-way itinerary with his wife and son.

Following the arrest, the document claims the defendant's wife told FBI agents who interviewed her that "her US visa was expiring" and so she and her son were "permanently moving back to Saudi Arabia", and her husband intended to do the same.

On 10 October, the day after Alfozan was arrested, his wife and son flew from San Francisco to Doha, Qatar. They travelled on a one-way business class ticket booked and paid for by a Saudi military official.
"Ultimately, the defendant has little incentive to remain in the United States to see this case through," the prosecutors argued.
The FBI investigation is ongoing.
Alfozan is scheduled to ‌appear ⁠in federal court in San Francisco later on Monday. If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (£188,000) fine.

articles.title: Exiled critic of Rwandan president found beheaded
articles.summary: Former army sergeant major Robert Kabera was a popular YouTuber and singer, who had sought asylum in Uganda.
body: Robert Kabera was a popular YouTuber and singer
A former Rwandan army sergeant major, who became an outspoken critic of President Paul Kagame, has been found beheaded in neighbouring Uganda.
Robert Kabera, 50, fled Rwanda after being accused of sexual assault, which he denied. He sought asylum in neighbouring Uganda, citing political persecution.
Ugandan police spokesperson Kituuma Rusoke on Monday said that Kabera's head had still not been recovered. His body was discovered by local residents on the outskirts of Kampala over the weekend.
The Rwandan government has not publicly commented on the killing. Several critics of Kagame have been killed, both in Rwanda and abroad.
His widow, Jeanne d'Arc Rwigema Uwizeye, told BBC Great Lakes in a written message that she now feared for her family's safety.
"It is scary. I feel crazy, the children and I don't have security," she said.
According to his family, Kabera had travelled to inspect a construction site about 45 km (30 miles) outside Kampala before his death.
Kabera built a public profile as a musician and YouTuber, attracting more than 144,000 subscribers to his channel, which featured over 800 videos, many criticising Kagame and his administration.
Reacting to news of his murder, exiled opposition group Rwanda National Congress (RNC) called for a thorough investigation and for those responsible to be brought to justice.
In a statement on X, the RNC said: "Today, his family is grieving, his voice is gone, and Rwandans in exile are confronting a terrifying question: where can we be safe?"
His death adds to concerns about the safety of Rwandan dissidents living in exile.
In 2014, Patrick Karegeya, a former Rwandan intelligence chief who helped set up the RNC, was found dead in his hotel room in Johannesburg, South Africa.

Karegeya fell out with President Paul Kagame and was arrested twice, serving an 18-month prison sentence for insubordination and desertion before fleeing to South Africa in 2007, where he became a vocal critic of the government.
Following his death, Kagame made remarks widely seen as a warning to other critics.
"Any person alive who may be plotting against Rwanda, whoever they are, will pay the price. Whoever it is, it is a matter of time," he said.
In 2019, South African authorities issued arrest warrants for two Rwandans accused of murdering Karegeya.

articles.title: Houthi missile strike on Yemen camp kills 50 security recruits, local authorities say
articles.summary: Three missiles hit a camp in government-controlled Shabwa province that officials say was being used as a training centre for new recruits.
body: Yemen's government said the missile strike killed recruits to its internal security forces (file photo)
More than 50 security personnel have been killed and 200 injured in a Houthi missile strike on a camp in Yemen's central province of Shabwa, local authorities say.

A spokesman for the Saudi-backed Yemeni armed forces said the Iran-backed group launched three ballistic missiles at al-Alam camp near Ataq city, which was being used as a training centre for recruits to the security forces and police.
The head of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, condemned what he called the "criminal attack" and promised a "firm response".
The Houthis' military spokesman said they had targeted "Saudi enemy concentrations".
Yemen's devastating civil war has flared up in recent months.
At the start of October, pro-government forces launched a major offensive that aims to retake territory in western Yemen that is controlled by the Houthis.

With air support from a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states, they managed to regain control of territory on the Red Sea coast that overlooks the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, which the Houthis captured in a surprise assault in September.
However, fierce fighting is continuing there, as well as around the besieged government-controlled city of Taiz, and to the north in Marib and al-Jawf provinces.
The Houthis have also responded to the Saudi air strikes by launching missiles and drones at airports, energy facilities and military bases in neighbouring Saudi Arabia.
Houthi missile attack on Yemeni presidential palace kills five, minister says
On Yemen's desert battlefield, a war with global consequences is being waged
'We are terrified but we want to get an education', say Yemeni schoolgirls
Monday's attack in Shabwa is one of the deadliest reported since the start of the escalation.

Shabwa province's media office said in a statement that ballistic missiles struck the Martyr Ahmed al-Sulaimani Training Centre, where recruits from several provinces were undergoing training to be members of the internal security forces. According to a preliminary assessment, 53 were killed and more than 200 injured, it added.
A video posted on social media appeared to show several bodies scattered across the ground.

Shabwa's deputy governor, Fahad al-Khalifi, told AFP news agency that hospitals in the province were overwhelmed and had been forced to transfer the most seriously wounded to neighbouring Hadramout and Aden, where the government is based. Some of them were in a critical condition, he said.
Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said the attack constituted a war crime because the internal security forces training centre was not a military target.

He also accused the Houthis of "attempting to fabricate a false media victory, boost the morale of its collapsing elements, and cover up the defeats and setbacks it is suffering across various combat axes".
The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said in a statement that the missiles targeted a gathering of "Saudi enemy" forces at al-Alam camp, which he said was run by Saudi officers.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities.

In a separate development, Houthi-run media reported that a Saudi air strike on a home in the Sahar district of the Houthi-controlled northern province of Saada on Sunday killed at least 10 people and injured 23 others, many of them women and children.
According to the Houthi-run health ministry in north-western Yemen, a total of 141 people had been killed in Saudi strikes over the past seven weeks.
The government's health ministry, meanwhile, said last week that at least 1,282 people had been killed in the conflict across Yemen since 6 August.
In Saudi Arabia, at least 19 people have been killed in Houthi attacks targeting the kingdom's airports since the beginning of October.

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

articles.title: Obama blasts federal probe of congresswoman Ilhan Omar as 'so appalling'
articles.summary: Obama says federal agents' search of the Democrat's home was an effort to intimidate a Trump critic.
body: Barack Obama has said congresswoman Ilhan Omar is under federal criminal investigation simply because she's an outspoken critic of the President Donald Trump.

"The full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president," the former US president wrote on X, calling the probe "so appalling".
The White House defended the inquiry, saying the justice department was "focused on restoring law and order".

Last week, homeland security agents searched the Minnesota Democrat's Washington DC home as part of an investigation into her immigration status. Born in Somalia, Omar moved to the US with her family as a child.
US media outlets have reported that the probe is tied to her American citizenship and whether she lied about her age when she arrived in the US in 1995.
Questions have been raised about whether the age listed on Omar's citizenship application differed from her actual birth date.
Obama said in his X post on Sunday that her father became a naturalised citizen when she was 17, and not yet legally an adult, which then gave her citizenship.

"Now the Administration is actively trying to deport Congresswoman Omar, seemingly based solely on the unsubstantiated theory that she was actually 18 when her father was naturalized, and therefore is not a citizen," he wrote.
"If this becomes the new normal," he added, "there's no reason to believe it will stop with her - or that future presidents, in either party, won't do the same."

According to the US Citizenship and Immigration Services, a child born outside of the US automatically becomes a citizen when he or she has at least one parent who is a citizen by birth or naturalisation, or he or she is under the age of 18, and is a lawful permanent resident living in the custody of a citizen parent.
White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis denied the investigation was politically motivated.
"Unlike Joe Biden, President Trump has not weaponized the Department of Justice against his political foes," she said in an emailed statement to the BBC.
"The Department is focused on restoring law and order and keeping Americans safe."
Trump has often argued that federal criminal investigations against him as he campaigned for re-election were politically motivated.

The investigation into Omar could lead to the justice department seeking to "denaturalise" her, or revoke her citizenship. It would have to prove there were material lies in the naturalisation process.
In 2023, Republicans removed Omar from the House Foreign Affairs Committee for comments and tweets she made about Israel, which drew bipartisan criticism.
Omar has said that Trump has targeted her for years with "baseless lies and smear campaigns" and called the investigation "the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation".
But Trump has said the investigation had "nothing to do" with him, while describing Omar as a "terrible person" and a "complainer".
Federal agents reportedly seized her phone, computers, notebooks and passport in the raid a week ago.

Her lawyers have demanded the government return her belongings, CBS News, the BBC's US partner, has reported, arguing in a letter sent on Friday that the seizure of property had violated restrictions put in place by a judge to protect her work as a federal lawmaker.

The lawyers also alleged agents did not duly notify Omar or the House of Representatives general counsel that a search would be taking place and kept her from contacting her attorney for more than an hour, according to CBS.

Democrats characterised the raid as the president attempting to interfere with the legislative branch of government. Republicans, meanwhile, have said Omar should be treated the same as anyone else under the law.

When Obama first ran for president, and throughout his two terms in the White House, Trump repeatedly raised questions about his citizenship, asserting he was not born on American soil and was disqualified from serving in office. Obama released two records proving he had been born in Hawaii.
Obama did not mention that history in his X post on Sunday.
