articles.title: US airman dies as daredevil descent goes wrong before Texas college football game
articles.summary: The game continued after the incident. The American Conference said the decision was made before his death was known.
body: A member of the US Air Force died after he fell while abseiling from the ceiling of a Texas stadium ahead of a college football game.

Footage shows the serviceman plummet feet first to the turf midfield at San Antonio's 170ft (52 metre) high Alamodome on Saturday during a ceremony ahead of the game between the University of Texas at San Antonio and the Naval Academy.
The airman, identified, external by the military as Sgt Ian Patterson, a Tactical Air Control Party instructor at Joint Base San Antonio, died in hospital.
The incident is being investigated. The game between the UTSA Roadrunners and the Navy Midshipmen continued as planned following the tragic incident.
A collegiate athletic association said the decision to press ahead with the fixture was made before the airman's death had been confirmed.
"We extend our deepest condolences to his family, friends, teammates and members of the 57th Wing," the American Conference, external said in a statement.
US Air Force Brig Gen Scott Mills said in a statement issued by Nellis Air Force Base: "This tragedy is felt deeply across the 57th Wing.
"Tech Sgt Patterson and his service mattered immensely to our wing."
Patterson, from Fort Stewart, Georgia, had served in the US military for 15 years, according to Nellis Air Force Base.
He held multiple military decorations and was in 2022 named the Air Force Special Warfare Enlisted Instructor of the Year at the Headquarters Air Force level.

UTSA president Taylor Eighmy said: "I want to extend my deepest and most heartfelt sympathies to the service member's family, his fellow airmen, squadron and all those whose lives have been touched by this heartbreaking tragedy."

articles.title: Personal attacks fire up debate before Brazil's run-off vote
articles.summary: The race heats up just days before the run-off between the left-wing incumbent and his right-wing challenger.
body: Flávio Bolsonaro and Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva are competing for the presidency in a run-off election due on Sunday
Brazil's left-wing President, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his right-wing rival, Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, have clashed in a debate held one week before the run-off presidential election.
Polls suggest the two candidates are neck and neck and the televised debate was hailed as a chance for both to sway undecided voters.
But the showdown was marked by personal attacks and analysts have warned that its aggressive tone may increase the abstention rate further.
In the first round of voting, held on 4 October, Bolsonaro defied opinion polls by securing a narrow lead over Lula.
Sunday's debate was the first of two before the vote. The second is planned for Friday, just two days before polls open.

Flávio Bolsonaro is standing for the Liberal Party after his father, Jair Bolsonaro - who governed from 2018 to 2022 - was sentenced to more than 20 years in prison for plotting to overthrow Lula after the latter beat him in the 2022 election.
The younger Bolsonaro won 47% of the vote in the first round, compared with Lula's 45.2%, with both falling short of the 50% of the valid votes needed to stave off a decisive second round.

Since the return to democracy in 1988, there has been no instance in which the candidate who lost in the first round went on to win in the second but Lula has told his supporters that he will "win in extra time".
Analysts consulted by BBC News Brasil were struck by how much the debate was dominated not by issues but personal attacks.
Yuri Sanches from pollsters AtlasIntel said it was a debate in which no policies were discussed and there were no rational arguments.
"The independent voter, who is sometimes against Bolsonaro and sometimes against the Workers' Party [of Lula], came out of it with a very negative impression."
Lucas Aragão from political analysis firm Arko Advice said Bolsonaro had appeared calmer during the debate and seemed to have managed to "get under Lula's skin".

Rafael Cortez from consulting firm da Tendências Consultoria, however, argued that Lula had managed to score a goal when he said he would open up his financial and phone records and those of his family to judicial scrutiny, and challenged his rival to do the same before Sunday's run-off.
Many observers criticised the format of the debate, which was described as chaotic at times, with each of the candidates pacing around the TV studio as the other was speaking.
One heated exchange saw Bolsonaro telling Lula he should come stand next to him so that the two could talk.

Referring to alleged links between the senator and paramilitary vigilante groups, Lula said "I don't want to be close to you", and that he wanted to maintain "distance from the Bolsonaro family" and "the militia".
Bolsonaro, who has dismissed the allegations as fake news, in turn tried to bait Lula by saying, "On second thoughts, maybe it's better to keep my distance so that my wallet isn't stolen."
He also accused the Workers' Party of being corrupt, holding up the palm of his hand on which he had scribbled "CORRUPTO" (Portuguese for "corrupt).
Bolsonaro had highlighted the initials for the Workers' Party on his hand
"Take a piece of paper and a pen and jot down 'corrupt' and you'll see that it has two letters in the middle here together," he said, pointing to PT, the initials of the Workers' Party in Portuguese.
Bolsonaro, who is campaigning on a iron-fist approach to crime, challenged Lula to explain why crime rates had gone up during his four years in power.
He also alleged, without providing any evidence, that "the majority of convicts vote for Lula".
Lula shot back with a thinly veiled reference to Flávio's convicted father, Jair, saying; "I wish it was 100%, even your father".

articles.title: Deadly fire at Canada military base moved a kilometre 'in 30 to 60 seconds'
articles.summary: The blaze that killed four men and injured dozens of others spread with alarming speed, accounts suggest.
body: Carney: 'Canada must now serve' service members killed in fire
The fire that killed four members of the Canadian military and injured dozens of others on Saturday spread with alarming speed, accounts suggest.
It broke out in a grassy training area at a base in the province of Alberta and spread rapidly due to strong winds.

"The fire was 1km (0.6 miles) away when the wind shifted," said Maj-Gen Wade Rutland, commander of the 1st Canadian Division of the Canadian Armed Forces. "It is not normal for a fire to move a kilometre in 30 to 60 seconds."

Prime Minister Mark Carney described it as "one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime". Officials have ruled out the possibility of "any terrorist activity" being to blame for the fire.
The blaze began at about 16:00 (22:00 GMT) on Saturday at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, one of the country's busiest military training bases.
The BBC has confirmed that Sgt Morgan Wong, Pte Shaun Farrell, Pte Aidan Goulding and Pte Hayden Lykkemark have died.
Of the 39 injured people receiving care in hospital, at least 19 are in a critical condition.

Warren Thirsk, an emergency department doctor at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told Canadian broadcaster CBC that the number of patients involved in the incident had "completely overwhelmed" healthcare facilities in Wainwright.
What we know so far about deadly fire at Canadian military base
Tributes are being paid to the servicemen who died.
Patricia Farrell, the mother of Shaun Farrell, wrote on Facebook that it was "with heavy hearts that we share the news that our son, Shaun Farrell, has passed away to be with our Heavenly Father".

Wong received a tribute from the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, of which he was part. The regiment was "deeply saddened", it wrote in a Facebook post of its own. It sent "heartfelt condolences to [the group's] families, friends, and fellow soldiers".

The mother of Goulding, Sonia Monk, said her late son was an exceptional athlete and a natural leader. "He was always the guy who kept everybody's spirits up," she told CBC. "He really was the light of my life."
Watch: Incident at Canadian military base 'unheard of', says local mayor
In account of Saturday's events, Rutland told reporters that members of the infantry had been conducting "high-intensity combat training with live munitions" at a grenade range and attack range.
He told reporters that officials knew about the fire on the base for several hours, but it was decided that training "could carry on for a certain amount of time".
"I spoke to my commander last night, and he said within 30 seconds to a minute they saw no fire, and then there was a fire right on top of them," Rutland said.
Rutland said it was not yet known what exactly caused the fire.

Some witnesses had said they had heard explosions, fuelling speculation that oil and gas infrastructure may have been hit and sparked the fire. But Rutland said authorities "do not believe this [incident] to be a result of any oil and gas infrastructure".
The Canadian Armed Forces has said that "while the incident remains under investigation, at this time, there are no indications that it was the result of any terrorist activity".
Forecasters had issued a wind warning on Saturday for large parts of Alberta, predicting wind gusts of up to 90km/h (66mph), Canadian broadcaster CBS said.
According to Rutland, the investigation may take at least a month.

Wainwright, about 130 miles east of Edmonton, Alberta's capital, is one of the main bases used by the Canadian military for live-fire training exercises, and it houses troops from Canada and allied countries.
About 690 military personnel and 300 civilian workers are on site on a typical day.

articles.title: Possible wreckage of Amelia Earhart's plane likely to be trees, say researchers
articles.summary: Researchers travelled to a remote Pacific Island to confirm whether an object first spotted on satellite imagery in 2020 solved the mystery of the pilot's disappearance.
body: A satellite image of the so-called Taraia Object, which some had hypothesised could have been Amelia Earhart's plane, in a lagoon on Nikumaroro
Researchers inspecting an object that some thought could have been the wreckage of Amelia Earhart's plane on a remote Pacific island say it is likely to be washed up trees.

The team travelled to a lagoon in the Taraia Peninsula on Nikumaroro, Kiribati, to confirm whether a shiny object first spotted on satellite imagery in 2020 solved the decades-long mystery of the pioneering pilot's disappearance.
But Purdue University, which has a leading role in the study, said the so-called Taraia Object "was likely a collection of large trees deposited along the peninsula's sandspit".
By the time the team arrived at the site a good portion of the debris had fragmented and washed away, leaving only a single Y-shaped segment, the university said.
Amelia Earhart disappeared over the Pacific Ocean while piloting her Electra plane in 1937

Images of the Taraia Object - which Purdue University said was visible in photography dating back to 1938 - led researchers to wonder if it was the remnants of a small aircraft sitting in shallow waters.
"This mystery has been ongoing for 90 years and the mystery continues," said project director Rick Pettigrew, speaking from near the site of the object.
"The island has been holding on to its secrets and it continues to do so. I think eventually someone will find conclusive evidence here," he added.
Earhart's plane vanished without a trace in 1937 on the third-to-last leg of her attempt to fly around the world.
She had already successfully flown from California across South America, Africa and Asia in her twin-engine Lockheed Electra when she arrived in Lae, Papua New Guinea.
Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan had planned to then travel towards Hawaii before returning to California.
But their plane vanished while trying to reach Howland Island, a remote uninhabited coral island about 400 miles (644km) from Nikumaroro, to refuel.
One theory is Earhart unintentionally navigated to Nikumaroro, where she ditched her plane and died a castaway.
The research team had travelled for five days by sea to reach Nikumaroro and was forced to spend several days on their ship following rough seas and strong winds, delaying their search on the island.
They spent four days onshore investigating the site.

articles.title: Catalonia's former rebel president can return to Spain, court rules
articles.summary: The court upholds a decision to lift an arrest warrant for Carles Puigdemont linked to the independence bid he led in 2017.
body: Puigdemont pictured during his only known return to Spain since fleeing, in 2024 - an appearance which prompted a police manhunt

Spain's Supreme Court has ruled the former president of Catalonia, Carles Puigdemont, can return without fear of arrest nearly a decade after going into self-imposed exile having led a failed independence bid.
The court upheld a decision to lift an arrest warrant for him linked to the referendum his regional government organised in 2017, in defiance of Madrid.

Direct rule was imposed on the region soon after the vote and Puigdemont fled to Belgium, where he has been based ever since - with a surprise appearance in Barcelona in 2024 prompting a police manhunt.
But the Spain to which he may return is much different from a decade ago, with Catalan independence now a marginal political issue.
Monday's ruling brings to an end a lengthy legal wrangle between the Spanish judiciary and the former Catalan president.

In 2024, Spain's socialist government introduced a controversial amnesty for dozens of Catalan politicians and activists who were involved in the secession drive, but the Supreme Court said Puigdemont and several of his colleagues should be excluded.
It argued this was because of the charges against them of alleged financial crimes around staging the referendum.

The Constitutional Court overruled that interpretation earlier this month, and on Monday the Supreme Court rejected an appeal by the far-right Vox party against lifting national arrest warrants for Puigdemont, as well as his former ministers Lluís Puig and Toni Comín, paving the way for their return to Spain.
Ex-Catalan leader ‘eludes police manhunt and flees Spain’
Catalonia's bid for independence from Spain explained
Spanish PM Sánchez calls early election after housing protests
Puigdemont was elected as a member of the European Parliament (MEP) in 2019 and to the Catalan parliament in 2024 as leader of the region's centre-right Together for Catalonia (JxCat) party.
He had campaigned in the south of France, where he held rallies attended by supporters who travelled across the border to see him.

Puigdemont is known to have made at least one brief return to Spain since leaving the country, addressing a crowd of supporters in Barcelona prior to disappearing and escaping back over the border to France before he could be detained.
While he was living in Waterloo, Belgium, nine of his former colleagues were jailed for their role in the events of 2017. They were released when the Spanish government pardoned them in 2021.
Puigdemont has remained an active political presence, travelling across Europe to espouse the Catalan independence cause and fiercely criticising Spain's democratic institutions.
In a video posted on social media just as the Supreme Court ruling was announced, Puigdemont spoke of his reasons for staying abroad.
"My role was to stir public opinion, internationalise the conflict and work from the heart of Europe to explain the reality of Spain," he said.
It is still not known when he might return to Spain.
Comín, his former regional minister for health, plans to travel this week to Madrid, where he is due to carry out administrative procedures linked to his status as an MEP.
The referendum sparked the country's biggest political crisis since democracy was restored following the death of Francisco Franco.

The banned vote was met with a heavy police crackdown. The region's separatist majority declared independence after the vote - Madrid then dissolved parliament, sacked its leaders and called a snap election.
But Catalan independence is now a relatively marginal issue in Spain, with housing and immigration dominating the political agenda.
The parliamentary support of Puigdemont's JxCat party was instrumental in allowing current Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez to form a new left-wing Spanish government after the 2023 election.
But within Catalonia, JxCat has been struggling, with a far-right, pro-independence party, Catalan Alliance, taking many of its voters.
And next month, Spain's general election could see the far right enter government for the first time.

articles.title: Meloni calls emergency meeting after weekend of violent clashes
articles.summary: More than 200 people were detained during two days of rioting in the city, Italian media reports.
body: More than 200 people were arrested across the weekend, according to Italian media
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni is set to hold an emergency security meeting on Monday after protests over the rising cost of living broke out into violent clashes in Milan.
More than 5,000 people gathered over the weekend. Police deployed tear gas and water cannons after protesters - many in masks - threw paving stones, bins and chairs at officers.
"To demonstrate is a right. To lay our cities to waste is not," Meloni said on Saturday, adding that "hooligans" had exploited the protests to "sow chaos".
Rioting and violence have broken out on the sidelines of mostly peaceful youth-led protests in other European countries including France, Spain and Albania.
Milanese Mayor Giuseppe Sala said he was worried it was a "new phenomenon" that "originates from an international scenario and therefore feeds itself".

Speaking to Italian news agency Ansa, he said he witnessed "smashed shop windows, looted stores, and frightened citizens", adding that "what happened here is what we are seeing in many cities around the world".
Clashes began on Saturday and continued into Sunday in Milan. More than 200 people were detained, 80% of whom were minors, Ansa reported.
The city's prosecutor's office has requested prison sentences for five adults arrested for looting, vandalism and resisting arrest, according to Italian news agency AGI.
Italian media reported that people - including police officers - were injured.
Violence between protesters and police also rippled into other cities in the north.
Meloni said people in Turin were detained while "carrying cobblestones and window-breaking hammers", while a train station in Bologna was closed as a precaution after similar disorder.
The prime minister - who is facing an election next year - also called on her political opponents to condemn the rioting.
"Do not be ambiguous about this," she said on X, explaining that condemnation must be "unanimous" because "any hesitation becomes justification".

Democratic Party leader Elly Schlein said her party had always condemned violence and that the rioting should not be used to stifle the voices of peaceful protesters across the country who are struggling to make a living, Ansa reported.

The violent disorder followed anti-government protests held by students in various Italian cities on Friday, and echoed similar unrest in neighbouring France, where hundreds of thousands took to the streets.

articles.title: Trump says suspension of Russia sanctions is to keep peace negotiations going
articles.summary: The US president blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect.
body: US President Donald Trump has said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table.

"I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said on his Truth Social messaging platform, adding that he didn't want to "do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table".
Trump blocked numerous sanctions on Russia on Friday night, two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky deepened.
Zelensky told NBC News on Sunday that siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin would be a "historic mistake".

Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev has responded to Trump's order by calling it "an important and truly historic moment". He said the sanctions, which were passed by the US Congress and signed into law by the US president in September, would have inflicted "serious damage" on the US and global market.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has described the suspension of the sanctions as a 60-day pause during which their potential impact on the US and global economies would be analysed.
In his Truth Social post, Trump also said Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did", adding "he could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now".
Zelensky has pushed for an end to fighting, and has repeatedly said that Putin doesn't want peace, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week.

Despite the international sanctions, Russia has still been able to export oil, much of it to China and India - often at attractive discounts. According to the think-tank Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), China has taken about half of Russia's crude exports, with India accounting for about 37%.

In remarks to a European Union summit, after Trump announced the deal to buy diesel from Russia and said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Putin, Zelensky said it was nice to be among "real leaders".
Ukraine's President Zelensky attended an EU leaders' summit in Brussels on Friday

Zelensky has repeatedly pushed for stringent sanctions to limit funding that Russia can use in its war effort. After the latest move from the US, however, he said he believed the Trump administration would lift more sanctions against Russia.
Ukraine and its European allies criticised Trump's plans to import Russian diesel to help lower US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war.
The deal, according to Zelensky, was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.

Concerns that Trump is siding with Russia have been heightened by disruption to Starlink, a US-provided satellite system used by Ukraine. That hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from Russian attacks.
Zelensky said US officials had linked speed restrictions to technical issues.
However, he said Ukraine had tested Starlink on EU territory and found it was operating at higher speeds.
Trump has denied both deliberately slowing down the network and a further accusation from Zelensky that the US had stopped sharing defence intelligence.
Trump waives several Russia sanctions as row with Zelensky intensifies
Zelensky says Ukraine has right to defend itself after Trump calls latest strikes a 'disgrace'
Russia accuses Ukraine of attacking oil refinery after Zelensky says strikes to resume

articles.title: Bangladesh says it was not informed of its citizens' execution by Saudi Arabia
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia said it executed two Bangladeshis last week for committing an "indecent act" in a mosque.
body: Two Bangladeshi nationals were executed over an "indecent act" in a mosque, Saudi authorities say
Bangladeshi authorities say they were not informed of the recent execution of two Bangladeshi nationals in the holy city of Mecca until after it had taken place, local media reports.

A Bangladeshi man and woman were executed last Wednesday after being convicted of committing an "indecent act" inside a mosque, according to the Saudi interior ministry. The ministry did not specify the nature of the offending act.
Bangladesh says it has reached out to the Saudi Arabian government to ask for more details about the case.
The two Muslim countries share a close relationship due to their religious affinity and strong economic ties.
More than three million Bangladeshis work and live in Saudi Arabia, mostly in low-paying jobs, and news of the double execution has raised public concern in Bangladesh.

According to the Saudi interior ministry, the two Bangladeshi nationals were convicted and sentenced to death under "tazir", which in Islamic law refers to punishments left to the discretion of the judge.
The ministry statement said they were handed the sentences because of the severity of the offence, and the fact that they violated the "sanctity" of the mosque.
Bangladesh has reached out to the Saudi government about the offences involved and legal proceedings in the case, said state minister for foreign affairs Shama Obaed Islam.
The government would consider next steps, such as the repatriation of the bodies, after getting information from Saudi authorities, Islam said.
She added that the government was committed to safeguarding the welfare and interests of Bangladeshis abroad.

The two executed Bangladeshis were included in a list of prisoners that Saudi Arabia had shared with Bangladesh, upon a request from the Bangladesh Consulate General in Jeddah - but that list did not indicate that the pair had been sentenced to death, the Daily Star reported.
This is not the first time that foreign nationals have been executed by Saudi authorities.
According to Amnesty International, the country has executed around 100 people this year, many of whom are foreigners convicted of drug offences.
In 2011, eight Bangladeshi men were publicly executed in the Saudi Arabian capital of Riyadh after they were found guilty of killing an Egyptian.

Earlier this month, Saudi Arabia overturned a death sentence handed to a Sri Lankan man over a comment he had made on Facebook, which had led to him being convicted of blasphemy. That decision came after the case sparked public outcry in Sri Lanka and spurred diplomatic efforts to seek clemency for the man.

articles.title: Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff survives shooting in Mumbai
articles.summary: Video published by several news outlets shows gunmen firing multiple shots at a car while it is moving past a crowd.
body: Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff did not sustain gunshot wounds in the shooting, police say
Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff has survived a shooting in Mumbai and has not sustained any gunshot wounds, according to Indian police who are investigating the incident.
The 36-year-old was shot at on Sunday evening, while he was in a car that was leaving a football club in the suburb of Juhu.
Several news outlets have published a video showing at least two gunmen firing multiple shots at close range at the front passenger seat of a car while it is slowly moving past a crowd.
The incident has heightened concern about the safety of public figures in India, with some killed or injured in targeted attacks in recent years.
"These attempts to intimidate people will not be tolerated, and we will put an end to this hooliganism," said Eknath Shinde, deputy chief minister of Maharashtra state, where Mumbai is located.
He paid a visit to Shroff after the shooting on Sunday evening, and said the actor and his mother had been left "shaken" by the attack.
Police said two people were injured in the shooting, including Shroff's driver, local media reported.
This is the latest in a string of attacks on some of the country's biggest public figures in recent years.
In 2024, police in India arrested two members of a criminal gang for a gun attack targeting the home of Bollywood actor Salman Khan.
That same year, influential Indian politician Baba Siddique was shot dead in Mumbai.
The son of two actors, Tiger Shroff made his acting debut in 2014 with the romance film Heropanti and went on to star in several films.
He is also a football enthusiast who plays for the professional football club Mumbay FC.

articles.title: How is the US economy really doing under President Trump?
articles.summary: Ahead of the midterms Trump has boasted about the performance of the US economy. BBC Verify looks at inflation, jobs and economic growth in the country.
body: President Donald Trump has been boasting about the performance of the US economy ahead of the midterm congressional elections, claiming he has boosted incomes, reduced inflation and created jobs.
Trump has repeatedly said: "We have the hottest country anywhere in the world."

While the overall US economy is faring better than many expected after Trump launched his sweeping "Liberation Day" tariffs in 2025, there's evidence those import taxes and the impact of the US-Israel war with Iran have pushed up inflation, with the harmful effects felt by most American households.
The US economy is also being helped by an AI investment boom, and could falter if that spending were to dry up.
So how does all this feel for the average American? BBC Verify has looked at whether the evidence supports the president's claims.
The overall US economy is growing at a respectable clip by the country's recent historic standards.
The latest data shows US GDP, external - which is how economists measure the size of the US economy - currently expanding at an annualised rate of 2.2%.
And it has increased by around 3.2% overall since the end of 2024, just before Trump took office for his second term.
That is more growth than any other member of the G7 group of leading economies over that period.

The US growth rate has been faster than was forecast by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), external in the immediate wake of Trump's announcement of a swathe of new tariffs on goods coming into the US on 2 April 2025.
It downgraded its forecasts at the time, citing the negative impact of Trump's import duties on investment and consumer spending.
Though it is important to note that Trump eased the tariffs considerably in the months that followed, reducing the impact that had initially been expected on the economy.
The US economy has also been heavily supported in recent years by American technology companies making massive investments in AI, including by constructing data centres around the country.
Spending on building data centres, external (excluding the IT hardware to go in them) by US businesses in August 2026 was $5bn, almost double the monthly rate when Trump returned to office.
Many American voters wanted to punish Joe Biden in the 2024 presidential election, holding him responsible for the pain caused by a significant spike in prices in the wake of the pandemic.
The current rate of US inflation, external is 3.7%.
That's still well down on the recent peak rate of 9% under Biden in 2022, but higher than the 3% rate that Donald Trump inherited in January 2025.
Economists estimate, external US inflation would have been lower without the new tariffs imposed by Trump since he returned to office.
While the impact of the Iran war on global energy prices, with the significant disruption to oil and fuel supplies from the Middle East, has also helped push up US domestic inflation.
The price of a gallon of diesel in the US, external - a fuel used not only by drivers but also widely in agriculture and industry - hit a record high of $6.52 in September.
The price of some grocery staples , externallike beef and coffee have risen since Trump returned to office, though the price of eggs has fallen.
And some US retailers have warned, external that rising energy prices caused by the Iran war will make producing food more expensive and raise prices at the till.
Average US household incomes are still rising under Trump.
The median income - after adjusting for inflation - rose 2.6% in 2025 to $87,460, the highest on record, external.
However, the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy (ITEP) think tank has estimated the combined effects of the following, external on US households:
- The expiry of extra government subsidies that had made health insurance cheaper for millions of Americans
- Higher-than-expected price rises during Trump's second term, including those linked to tariffs and the Iran war
ITEP's conclusion is that the middle fifth of households are, on average, around $1,700 worse off in 2026 than they would have been, while the poorest fifth are around $750 worse off.
The richest 1%, by contrast, are estimated to be an average of $12,560 better off than they woud have been, primarily because of Trump's tax cuts.
ITEP's estimates about the impact of tariffs on American households of different income levels are broadly similar to those of the Tax Foundation think tank, external.
Trump predicted his tariffs would result in America being "flooded with jobs", external as manufacturing firms set up new factories on US soil to avoid their products being taxed at the border.
Since he returned to the White House, an average of 34,000 jobs have been added to the economy each month.
​​But that is significantly down on the 122,000 jobs added each month in the final year of Biden's presidency, external.
And the number of Americans employed in manufacturing, external - 12.6 million in September 2026 - is slightly lower than it was when Trump's second term began.
However, the US unemployment rate remains relatively low, external at 4.2%, which is broadly where it was when Trump returned to the White House.

Part of the reason for this is Trump's immigration crackdown and deportation programme, which has reduced the size of the available US workforce, external and means a lower number of jobs need to be created each month to stop unemployment rising.
US government borrowing has increased in Trump's second term, partly driven up by his significant tax cuts.

The federal government deficit - the gap between its revenues from taxes and its spending - was $2 trillion in the year to September 2026, external. That's equivalent to around 6%, external of US GDP.
And the US deficit is projected to rise to above 8% of GDP by 2030, external.
That high rate of government borrowing is itself helping to boost US GDP growth.

The IMF has warned that excessive US government borrowing, external, which it uses to bridge the deficit, and its rapidly rising national debt are raising the risk of a future financial crisis in America. This would have a deeply damaging impact on most American households.
The growing deficit is also one of the reasons the US government gets charged more to borrow money in financial markets.
The 10-year US government bond yield has risen sharply since Trump returned to office in January 2025 and is now above 5%, the highest rate since the global financial crisis in 2007.
That increase in the market cost of US government borrowing also puts upward pressure on the interest rates on mortgages available to American households.
The interest rate on a new 30-year US mortgage has risen to 7.4%, external per year, up from 6.9% when Trump returned to the White House.

That's added to problems in the US housing market, making homes less affordable for new buyers. It has left many existing owners reluctant to move because doing so would mean giving up their cheaper mortgages, which they took out at lower rates, external and cannot take with them to a new property.
Data graphics by Erwan Rivault.

articles.title: Italy to deploy 500 troops to Milan after days of protests and looting
articles.summary: Government planning tougher security measures after protests over high cost of living descend into violence
body: Italy’s government is sending 500 soldiers to Milan as it vowed a “firm response from the state” after protests against the high cost of living descended into clashes with police, vandalism and looting, and ahead of further demonstrations planned on Saturday.

The government, led by the far-right prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, is also planning to swiftly approve tougher new security measures, including extending preventive detention for minors, cracking down on youth gangs and banning gatherings for people deemed a threat to public order, according to reports in the Italian press on Tuesday.

Police in Milan detained 271 young people after hooded youths set bins ablaze, ransacked shops and smashed windows, including in the area surrounding the city’s Duomo, during the unrest on Saturday and Sunday.
Police used teargas and water cannons to disperse the violent groups, who were on the fringes of an initially peaceful protest.
Of those detained, 32 have been arrested, including 23 minors and 13 foreign nationals, police said on Monday. A further 28 people were reported to judicial authorities.

Ansa reported that one of the security measures being considered is specifically aimed at second-generation immigrant youths, known as “maranza” – a slang term used to describe gangs of young people, usually coming from marginalised areas.
Many luxury stores in Milan’s fashion district have stayed closed amid fears of further unrest. Brands including Chanel, Tiffany ‌and Dior had removed merchandise from ‌their windows as a precaution.
Other stores ransacked included sports retailers Decathlon and Arc’teryx and mobile phone operator Vodafone, television footage showed.

“The government will respond firmly to these attacks on the state, ​including through measures aimed at curbing violence by minors,” the foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, who also serves as deputy prime minister, said after Meloni chaired a meeting with top security officials on Monday.

Meloni’s coalition, which is facing a general election next year, is reportedly planning tougher penalties for road blockades too, following days of protests in southern Italy by lorry drivers over fuel prices.

Meanwhile, Milan is bracing for further protests on Saturday after a new movement, called 17 October, emerged on social media saying it would demonstrate there and in other major Italian cities each Saturday afternoon “until this government of thieves collapses”.
“You are the violent ones,” the group said. “You, who denied us a future. Now, we are claiming that future ourselves.”

Opposition politicians often accuse the government of using security as a propaganda tool, arguing that Italy’s leaders do little to address core issues such as education, housing and living conditions in marginalised areas.
Related: Why are people protesting across Europe?

There were also tensions during protests at the weekend over the high cost of living in other northern Italian cities, ​including Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo ​and Turin, where 28 protesters were arrested, police said.

The disturbances echoed unrest in neighbouring France, where hundreds of thousands of people angered by rising living costs and declining public services took to the streets on Saturday in some of the country’s most violent protests in years.

articles.title: Fleeing the frontline: Yemeni families cross Red Sea to Djibouti as Houthi conflict rages
articles.summary: Their overland routes to safety blocked off, several thousand people have boarded boats to escape gunfire, bombing and a dire humanitarian situation
body: Abubaker Saeed was fishing in the Red Sea off Yemen’s coast last month when he noticed explosions in the distance. His mind turned immediately to his wife and two children, and he raced back to his home village of al-Wahijah.

Aircraft from the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemeni government forces had launched airstrikes in surrounding areas, targeting members of the Iran-aligned Houthi militia as its fighters approached the nearby port city of Mocha.
“They were bombing Houthis while Houthis were 1km away from us,” the 50-year-old recalled.

By the time he reached the shore, the rebels had arrived and were battling government forces on the ground. As Saeed tried to get to his house, he witnessed three people being shot and killed in the fighting.
He managed to make it through the havoc of bombings and shootings to reunite with his family in his house, where they hid as the fighting raged for 12 hours until the government forces withdrew.

When the fighting ended, Saeed decided it was no longer safe for his wife and children – aged nine months and five years – to stay in al-Wahijah. Because Houthis had taken control of all the overland routes to safer areas of Yemen, he had no option but to try to take his family across the Bab al-Mandab strait to Djibouti. They headed to the shore, about 1km from their house, carrying nothing but the clothes on their backs.
They boarded a boat with about 80 other people. The operators charged 100,000 Yemeni rials (about £320) a family, but let Saeed’s family travel despite having no money. The journey lasted nine hours.

Saeed is one of several thousand Yemenis who have fled into Djibouti in recent weeks. He is sheltering with other Yemeni nationals at the packed Markazi humanitarian site near the fishing town of Obock in the north-east of the country.
Pointing to his white T-shirt, the same one he wore while fleeing, he said: “I left everything behind.”

The renewed fighting in Yemen has created a dire humanitarian situation. More than 900 people have been killed, and at least 250,000 have been forced out of their homes since the beginning of August. The clashes exacerbated an existing crisis in the country, where the UN estimates that more than half the population needs humanitarian assistance.

“Ongoing fighting, insecurity and restrictions on movement are making it increasingly difficult to reach displaced communities and deliver assistance safely,” said Laila Al Amine, regional programmes director at the Prosper Global charity (formerly Mercy Corps), which is assisting displaced people in Taiz governorate, where more than 100,000 have sought refuge. “After more than a decade of conflict, families in Yemen should not have to keep running in search of safety.”

The governorate’s capital, Taiz, and Yemen’s south-western Red Sea coast, including the area around the Bab al-Mandab strait – a strategic global trade position at the intersection of Yemen, Djibouti and Eritrea – have all witnessed heavy fighting during the renewed conflict, as Houthi militia and the Yemeni forces battle for territory.
In recent weeks fighting has intensified around Taiz, the third-largest city in Yemen, as Houthis encircle it and take control of routes in and out of the city, raising fears of a siege.

On a recent sweltering day at the Markazi humanitarian site, families sat beside mounds of their belongings, including mattresses, jerrycans and buckets. Children played on a swing and women in burqas chatted in clusters.
A mile away from the humanitarian site, a few hundred Yemenis staggered towards it carrying aid packages from a government warehouse.

Inside a building at the site where she and her family are staying, Madinah Abdullah painfully recollected surviving airstrikes and gunfire in her home city of Mocha in September, then fleeing after Houthis took over from retreating government forces. “We were living on the frontline,” said the 43-year-old.

Abdullah said Houthis forcibly recruited boys and young men, or accused them of working with government forces. She was especially worried the group would take her 16-year-old son. “I was afraid Houthis would see my son,” she said.
They hid until an opportune moment presented itself, and they and their seven other family members took a fishing boat to Djibouti with about 40 other people.
“Life in Mocha was very good before the conflict, but Houthis disrupted everything,” said Abdullah, who used to work with an aid organisation.
In Markazi, Yemenis found a site that was already hosting refugees, including fellow nationals who arrived after the outbreak of the civil war in 2014.

As of 8 October, the number of new Yemeni arrivals had reached 3,807, according to Yemen’s office for assistance to refugees and disaster victims. Mahdi Osman, coordinator at the agency, said there was increasing pressure on shelter capacity, water supply, sanitation facilities, food assistance and healthcare services. “The main challenge lies in the gap between the rapid pace of arrivals and the resources available to receive newly arrived refugees and meet their essential needs,” he said.

“Djibouti continues to demonstrate solidarity with people forced to flee conflict, despite its limited resources. We call on the international community to stand alongside the government of Djibouti to ensure that every person arriving in the country has access to effective protection, shelter and essential services.”

Yemen’s civil war erupted in 2014 when Houthis took control of the country’s capital, Sana’a, and the government. In response, a coalition led by neighbouring Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates carried out a military campaign to reinstate the Yemeni government.

A ceasefire facilitated by the UN was established in 2022 and was mostly adhered to until July, when Houthis fired drones and missiles towards Saudi Arabia in response to what they said were Saudi airstrikes on the international airport in Sana’a aimed at preventing an Iranian plane carrying Yemenis from landing.

In early September Houthis launched a lightning offensive along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, seizing key positions around the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait, which had become an important route for Saudi oil exports because of disruptions in the strait of Hormuz caused by the US war against Iran.

Houthi militias have also launched attacks on Saudi airports, tankers and oil facilities. On 10 October, a missile attack by the rebel group on King Khalid International airport in the capital, Riyadh, killed 13 people. Experts fear the escalating conflict could draw additional countries into the crisis.
For many Yemenis who have fled to Djibouti, the recent displacement is yet another mark of the war on their lives.

Aisha Ismail still has a bullet in her leg from a shooting that happened at the onset of the civil war. She fled to Djibouti in September with her sister and their elderly father, who has a hearing impairment. “War, gunfire and bombing,” she said of the factors that had driven them to leave their home.

The 33-year-old added: “We just ran away because we have no men to protect us. My father is an old man and he is now 85 years old and we have no brother or uncle. Out of fear, we just ran away without taking anything. We left everything behind. All our belongings.”
From their home town of Dhubab, just north of the Bab al-Mandab strait, they trekked for miles to find a boat to Djibouti, and finally made the journey across with more than 100 other people.

Ismail used to sell potatoes to sustain herself, her father and her sister. She bemoans that although food is distributed at the site, it’s never enough. “The last time I ate something was yesterday,” she said one late morning.

Saeed is often occupied with volunteering at a water collection point, where he helps children and other vulnerable people draw water from a tap, “so that everyone has a fair opportunity to access water without confusion”.
Like those of many others at the site, his thoughts often return to his home in Yemen. “My hope,” he said, “is that the war will end so that I can return home with my family and live in peace”.

articles.title: Alberta voters reject plan for referendum to leave Canada
articles.summary: Result is a victory for prime minister Mark Carney and supporters of Canadian unity
body: Voters in Canada’s Alberta have overwhelmingly rejected a proposal to begin a process towards independence, delivering a victory for the prime minister, Mark Carney, and supporters of Canadian unity.
With more than 1.5m votes counted, 76% supported remaining in Canada, while close to 24% backed beginning a process toward separation, according to unofficial results from Elections Alberta.
Carney, who grew up in Edmonton, Alberta’s capital, said: “Albertans made a clear choice. They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other. Above all, Albertans chose Canada.”

He said the result would allow Canadians to move forward together and accelerate efforts to diversify trade, develop major infrastructure projects and make Canada a global energy powerhouse, with Alberta at its centre.

Alberta’s separatists, however, saw a silver lining. “We don’t have the final results. I think the numbers are going to fluctuate, but it is fair to say that at least a quarter of Albertans feel that Alberta needs to be treated better,” said Keith Wilson, a leader of the separatist movement.

The Alberta premier, Danielle Smith, welcomed the early results, saying they showed widespread support for remaining in Canada. “Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada,” Smith posted on social media.

Even though the vote was not explicitly about independence – a point that frustrated separatists – the ballot question nonetheless exposed divisions in Alberta’s politics and raised questions about the durability of national unity.

Delays at roughly 100 of the 1,400 at polling stations across the province pushed results back by more than two hours, but shortly after polls closed on Monday evening the results suggested a decisive win for those looking to remain in Canada.
Related: ‘This is not poker’: Alberta goes to polls in referendum that has exposed divisions, not least among separatists

The separation question – whether to remain in Canada or begin a legal process that could lead to a second vote – was one of 10 put to Albertans on Monday. The others covered issues including immigration, healthcare, education and the province’s constitutional powers. Elections Alberta said the remaining results could take days to count.
In the days leading up to the vote, provincial leaders and federal politicians crisscrossed the province to make the case for a unified country.

Carney warned against a vote from residents of the oil-rich province simply looking to “send a message” to the federal government. “A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and Canadians,” he told an energetic crowd last week.
The Conservative leader, Pierre Poilievre, whose parliamentary seat is in the province, told a crowd of supporters that Albertans were not “quitters”.

“To those people who are thinking about taking out their frustration on the current government by voting for separation in the referendum, I say this: Canada is more than a government,” he said. “It is a people, a flag, a land, a history and a promise.”

Data from Elections Alberta indicated roughly 43% of eligible voters – or 1.3 million Albertans – had already cast ballots before Monday’s vote through advance voting and mail-in ballots. That figure pointed to a potentially higher turnout than the province’s last referendum in 2021.

Smith’s tenure as leader of the United Conservative party is due in large part to separatists within the party who ousted her predecessor, Jason Kenney. In recent months she has tried to placate both the separatists and federalists in the party, in a province where a majority is not interested in secession.
The referendum became a political liability for Smith’s party, whose popular support has tumbled in recent months, including with the loss of a one-time conservative stronghold in a byelection.
Still, members of the separatist movement told the Guardian they would continue their push for independence.

In an interview before the results, the Calgary mayor, Jeromy Farkas, a staunch opponent of the independence movement, said the city’s “best future is here, as a Canadian city”, amid fears that uncertainty could lead to capital flight.

“I am Canadian because I’m Canadian, not in a transactional way and regardless of the flavour of prime minister,” Farkas said. “And I’m going to continue to make the case for how our future is strongest together, because no result will permanently put this to bed. “The separatist movement sees this as a long-term project.”

articles.title: Serbian prosecutor who investigated Belgrade Trump tower project ‘targeted with spyware’
articles.summary: Apparent attempt to hack Rade Bajić’s iPhone comes amid efforts to undermine landmark criminal case
body: A Serbian prosecutor who investigated the authorities’ allegedly illegal scheme to help the Trumps build a tower in Belgrade has been targeted with advanced spyware, expert analysis indicates.
Related: Revealed: Serbian ruler’s secret role in ‘illegal’ effort to help Trump business

The finding suggests a disturbing new element in the authoritarian Serbian regime’s campaign to undermine what is believed to be the first criminal case related to global moneymaking drive of the US president’s family, which critics describe as a “pay to play” scheme trading the Trump administration’s favour for business opportunities.
Rade Bajić, the targeted prosecutor, said: “In my opinion, my involvement in this case was the sole reason for this unlawful spyware attack.”

Analysts at the Citizen Lab, a digital forensics laboratory, have not so far established who was behind the attack but the Serbian regime has previously been caught using spyware against its opponents.

News of the alleged hack follows the Guardian’s revelations last week that Aleksandar Vučić, Serbia’s president, personally ordered that a cherished site in Belgrade be stripped of its legal protection so it could be handed over for a $500m Trump hotel and tower. Vučić, one of the Balkans’ most influential nationalists, hosted the US president’s son Donald Jr – “dear Don”, as he calls him – and son-in-law Jared Kushner as he ingratiated himself with the Trumps.

At the weekend, Vučić responded to the Guardian’s revelations about his role in the scandal by confirming details of a previously secret meeting. He indicated he had done nothing wrong. “I fought for my people,” he said. “And that’s what I’ll continue to do in the future.”

Last year prosecutors brought a landmark indictment against senior members of Vučić’s regime, accusing them of abusing their office to unlawfully strip the General Staff building – a monument to Serbia’s recent difficult history – of its protected status. They face years in jail if convicted.

Kushner, who was leading the Trump Belgrade development, called off the plans after the charges were made public. Vučić vowed reprisals, denouncing the prosecutors, including Bajić, a member of the specialised organised-crime unit that brought the indictment.

Bajić has said he was taken off the case without explanation shortly before the indictment was published. He went on to address one of the rolling protests against the regime triggered by widespread corruption, telling demonstrators in February: “The law will be equal for all.”
In August, Bajić received a message from Apple saying it had “detected a targeted mercenary attack against your iPhone”.
Citizen Lab researchers, who have been analysing Bajić’s phone, said this was “a high confidence indicator that his device was likely targeted with mercenary spyware, such as Pegasus”.

Working with the Share Foundation, a Serbian rights group, they previously identified spyware attacks against anti-government protesters. In at least one case, the Citizen Lab analysts discovered Pegasus on a protester’s phone. “A zero-click infection with Pegasus spyware would not have been visible to the target, and would give the Pegasus attacker total access to the device,” they said of that discovery.

The Guardian’s Pegasus Project revealed how journalists, activists, politicians and others have been targeted by governments using the spyware. NSO Group, the Israel-based company that makes Pegasus, has been approached for comment.

Vučić, who stepped down late last month and called snap elections for 25 October, hoping to prolong his 12-year rule by switching from president to prime minister. He has been approached for comment, as has the prosecutors’ unit, which has said it may bring more charges in the General Staff building case.

Representatives of the Trumps and Kushner have denied they engaged in “pay to play” arrangements and said they were not involved in the Serbian authorities’ decision to strip the building of its protected status.

articles.title: US gave us no warning of Russian strikes on Kyiv power plants, Zelenskyy says
articles.summary: Ukrainian president accuses Washington of ‘denial of reality’ in continuing row with Trump over apparent support for Moscow
body: Ukraine did not receive a warning from the US about an impending Russian missile attack on Sunday evening, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, reviving concerns that Washington is withholding intelligence to bully Kyiv into capitulating to Moscow.

Yuri Ihnat, a spokesperson for the Ukrainian air force, said on television on Monday morning that Ukraine had not received a warning before a Russian missile barrage hit power plants in Kyiv at about 11pm. Earlier, a Ukrainian government official had told the Guardian the US had not warned the capital about the impending missile strike.
Ukraine did receive a warning before a subsequent strike, at 3am, Ihnat added.

“Once again, Russia launched a ballistic missile attack in multiple waves throughout the night, and once again, there was no warning from our partners,” Zelenskyy wrote in a social media post on Monday morning.

“When the supply of missiles for Ukrainian air defence is blocked, and Russia receives sanctions relief or delays, it is, unfortunately, a denial of reality on the part of our partners,” the president added.
Zelenskyy is grappling with recent US moves benefiting the Russian president, Vladimir Putin.

On Friday, Donald Trump waived a sweeping package of sanctions on Russia, telling Congress the pause on the legislation, named after the late senator Lindsey Graham and passed by both chambers, was in the national interest. Ukraine has also complained of slowed deliveries of PAC-3 air defence missiles from the US.

The US president wrote on Truth Social on Sunday: “My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.
“Zelenskyy doesn’t care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him … he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did.”

Trump also told reporters on Monday that he would consider a trilateral meeting with Russia and China. He said: “We ‌would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearisation. If ‌President Xi wants to have it, I’d ​have it.”

For years, the US has warned Ukraine before Russia launched ballistic missiles, giving authorities several minutes to sound alarms and allow civilians to reach shelters before the strikes hit. However, Ukraine has said it was not warned on at least three days in the past week before missiles were launched, amid a public quarrel between Zelenskyy and Trump.

Speaking in the early hours of Monday on a trip to Samarkand, Uzbekistan, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said: “If it happened last night, I don’t know exactly. I know a few nights ago there was a software problem involving their early warning system.”

US officials have not previously mentioned a software glitch in the early warning system. In at least one case, Ukrainian officials had been told that bad weather over southern Russia had obscured preparations for the missile launch. Rubio said the military’s European Command was looking into the strikes.

The US has maintained plausible deniability as services and programmes provided to support Ukraine have suddenly begun to fail. The Trump administration has denied that it throttled services in Ukraine for Starlink, the satellite internet service run by Elon Musk that is used both on offensive drones and anti-air weapons by Ukraine.

Ukraine has also said US weapons delivered through the PURL scheme, where Europe purchases US weapons then delivers them to Ukraine, have been delayed. The Trump administration reportedly threatened Kyiv with a slowdown in crucial weapons deliveries unless it stopped striking Russian oil refineries.
On Sunday, Ukraine launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia in one of its largest aerial attacks of the war, setting fire to an oil export terminal and a depot in St Petersburg.

The Russian barrage on Sunday evening hit 28 substations and other critical energy facilities, depriving more than 500,000 people of electricity, heat and running water, Zelenskyy said on social media. Russia has sought to disrupt daily life in Ukraine by attacking trains, shopping centres, fuel stations and supermarkets, among other sites.
Russia fired 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region, Zelenskyy said, and officials in the capital reported that a 21-year-old woman had been killed.

Later drone strikes on a public park in the north-eastern Kharkiv region killed six people, including young children. The regional governor, Oleg Synegubov, said on Telegram that three of the dead in the attack on Nova Vodolaha were children, including one in a pushchair. Seven children were among the 14 wounded. Police posted pictures showing damaged playground equipment.

Synegubov condemned “another terrorist act by the Russian Federation”, saying “the enemy strikes a recreational park in the middle of the day, knowing that there is no military infrastructure there at all”.

Pope Leo XIV spoke by phone with Zelenskyy on Monday to discuss the embattled city of Oleshky in Ukraine’s Kherson region, according to a Vatican statement. He told the Ukrainian president that he had asked Putin for a humanitarian ceasefire during a call with the Russian leader on Friday.

Residents of Oleshky face a worsening humanitarian crisis, with shortages of food and medication, as they are caught in the crossfire between Russian and Ukrainian troops. The Vatican said that Leo had expressed deep concern about conditions in the city and sought a ceasefire to permit aid deliveries and evacuations.
The call to Zelenskyy came two days after Leo, 71, was discharged from a hospital in Rome where he underwent a lung cancer operation on Tuesday.
The Kremlin said on Friday it had explained to Leo what it called “the Kyiv regime’s responsibility for the difficult humanitarian situation”.

articles.title: Tuesday briefing: Can Andy Burnham beat Britain’s headphone dodgers?
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: The prime minister’s campaign against noisy passengers has struck a chord with commuters. Whether anyone hears him remains to be seen.
body: Me again, back from the October school holiday (a week in glorious Wales, thanks for asking) and ready to hear your commuter woes. For our prime minister, it’s “one of the most annoying things on public transport”: maybe you’re trying to work, or read, or you’ve finally got your kid to sleep, when someone starts blasting sound from their phone at full volume.

As I sign off this First Edition en route from Glasgow to London (the things I’ve heard on this commute, against my will, I’ll save for another newsletter), I’m hoping everyone has been paying attention.

I’m struck by how few voices there have been suggesting Burnham should be concentrating on more important matters. It seems to me that other people’s noise, and other inconsiderate behaviour on public transport, has become shorthand for wider concerns about social cohesion, generational conflict and political fragmentation. Put simply, we are all making much more noise, and have become much worse at listening to what anyone else is actually saying. For today’s newsletter, I spoke to a bus driver, a transport expert and a cultural critic to find out more. That’s after the headlines.

France | The prime minister has said he has asked regional authorities to impose partial curfews in some cities after the government admitted police had “lost control” in several places during violent weekend protests around the country.
UK politics | Andy Burnham has told officials to rip up their plans for how to fix Thames Water and present him with more radical options for what to do with the stricken company.

Yemen | At least 53 people have been killed in a Houthi ballistic missile attack on a training camp for Yemeni government forces in the largest single loss of life since the country’s civil war reignited in September.
Israel | Israeli police have detained 10 people in a rare raid against settlers, after a weekend of extreme violence in the occupied West Bank including an attack on US photojournalist Heidi Levine.
Reform | Nigel Farage undermined his own claims that a £5m gift was for security when he referred to the money as a reward for Brexit, according to one of his closest aides.

When Andy Burnham launched his crusade against unnecessary noise and antisocial behaviour on public transport with a chatty Instagram post recorded on a morning train into Manchester Piccadilly, my first thought was: “I bet he didn’t upload that on the dodgy onboard wifi.”

The prime minister’s sights were set on the phenomenon described as “loudcasting” or “headphone dodging” – but you don’t need a specialist term, because you know it when you hear the passenger next to you blasting Facebook slop on loudspeaker.

Alongside a nationwide campaign encouraging people to plug in their headphones and “share the carriage, not the noise,” Burnham announced new guidance to help local transport authorities introduce fines of up to £100 for nuisance behaviour like vaping, littering and playing loud music or videos on buses. Train operating companies already have powers to impose fines of up to £1,000 for antisocial behaviour.
If you’re grinding your molars at the thought, you’re not alone. A hefty majority of Britons, about 88% according to recent polling, consider it unacceptable to play music out loud on a train.
Who will actually enforce the rules?

It’s still unclear how these new rules would be enforced. Government officials have reassured bus drivers that they won’t be expected to police passengers themselves. That job will fall on transport safety officers or police officers.

Mark, a bus driver in central London, tells me he and his colleagues simply don’t have the capacity to help. He spends his working life in the glass cabinet at the front of the vehicle. He can’t hear every noise or spot every puff of vape smoke on the top deck, and, as well as navigating the city traffic, he already has other things to focus on, such as fare-dodging.

Mark’s route has become noisier in recent years, though he’s keen not to point out “it’s an all-ages” issue, and not to lay the blame solely with younger passengers. He doubts whether Burnham can isolate the problem to public transport. “It’s a whole society thing: being kinder and more aware of their environment.”
“It’s not workable without resources,” he says. “I don’t really see how it would be enforceable: you can’t have someone on every bus and train.”
Here lies the difficulty: fines for nuisance noise on trains are already vanishingly rare, with offenders able to shut up or leave the carriage before enforcement arrives.

The number of British Transport Police (BTP) officers has fallen by more than 10% over the past two years. The people left to challenge the noisy doom-scroller are, therefore, you and me. Transport for London, for example, has done some great work on bystander intervention, suggesting straightforward ways to interrupt bad behaviour without putting yourself in danger, but many of us would think twice about confronting a stranger in the confines of a moving vehicle.
Is this a crackdown on bad behaviour, or a distraction from worse problems?

Not everyone is impressed by the scale of the response. Sharon Graham, general secretary of Unite – a woman resolutely resistant to hoping, again – described the new policy as “well-meaning but wholly inadequate” to tackle the “avalanche of escalating abuse” faced by the transport workers she represents.

“There has been a massive escalation in reported assaults on public transport across the country,” says our transport correspondent Gwyn Topham, who reported earlier this month on the growing number of verbal and physical assaults faced by transport workers and passengers. In my previous incarnation as Scotland correspondent, I wrote about bus driver Keith Rollinson, who died at Elgin bus station after a violent assault by a teenage passenger.

Thoughtlessly broadcasting your TikTok scrolling is at the other end of the spectrum, but there’s an argument that antisocial behaviour exists on a continuum, and that a “nip it in the bud” approach might prevent more serious problems from escalating. Zero tolerance policing of course has a mixed record – and if you detect Tony Blair vibes here, so do I. Dropping a grand for loudcasting your tunes has more than a whiff of New Labour’s respect agenda and the classist asbo culture it ushered in, which singularly failed to tackle antisocial behaviour at its roots.

Still, there’s much to be said for elevating the issue from shared eye-rolls to official tannoy announcements. This is a policy that is going to appeal hugely to commuters, Gywn predicts, and when we are speaking he points out that the article about the campaign launch has been most-read across the Guardian website throughout the morning. “What he’s done well is to acknowledge an everyday irritation, that doesn’t cost a lot of money to fix, but can hopefully alter public behaviour.”
Can telling people to behave better work?

Gentle nudges towards more respectful behaviour, rather than sledgehammer fines, have made a difference historically, writer Dan Hancox tells me. His latest book, Multitudes, is about crowd behaviour, and recalls “a real moral panic” in the early 2010s over teenagers playing tinny MP3s aloud from basic mobile phones.

Dan could see why people found this irritating, but defended it at the time: “It was a rare example of sharing of music as a social adhesive, at a moment when David Cameron was introducing austerity and the spaces in which young people could gather together were being shut down.”
Crucially, within a couple of years the behaviour had died down again, as often happens after the initial buzz around new technology and the social pressure points they create.

But this phenomenon of people playing video out loud on their phones has got noticeably worse in the last couple of years, he believes, and, as I match Dan’s anecdotal experience with my own, it’s not all about the young ones this time. Indeed, younger travellers seem more likely to rely on noise-cancelling headphones – which some audiologists have raised concerns over potential links to auditory processing problems.

So why are otherwise apparently mature adults broadcasting their content and calls on the bus? The notion that people have “forgotten how to behave” since the Covid lockdown is one that Dan refutes. “It feels like an easy answer for something that is much more complex,” he says. “But it didn’t go on for that long, and the really remarkable thing about human beings is how quickly and elastically they bounce back to their previous sets of behaviours.”
The more boring answer, he suggests from his own research, is that as 5G makes watching videos easier to do wherever we are – people are simply seizing that opportunity.

But crowd psychology tells us that other people’s propensity to broadcast noise has a minimal effect on our own behaviour. “People’s pre-existing values and social mores are incredibly robust and are unlikely to change based on the behaviour of a complete stranger,” says Dan. And this makes it much more susceptible to the kind of nudge messaging over the train tannoy that Burnham is proposing.

In my own experience of antisocial behaviour on public transport, it seems that two things can be true at once: there’s a growing anxiety that this indicates an unravelling of the social contract, and in the main our interactions with fellow passengers often reassure us this is not, in fact, the case.

It’s possible that anxiety about strangers and the malign influence of the crowd arises at moments of wider pressures, says Dan. “When people are worried about paying the rent or feeding their families, as wars in the wider world rock our sense of stability and faith in human beings, our suspicion of the random person on the bus grows.

“But my day-to-day experience of life in a big and supposedly alienating city like London tells me people want this kind of spontaneous connection more than ever, and it’s a joy when it happens. Even if it’s just a few warm words exchanged with a stranger at the bus stop, on the train or in the shops – this is what it means to live in a society.”
Next week, the chancellor, John Healey, will deliver his first budget. We want to hear what you think the chancellor should do, so email us at first.edition@theguardian.com.

Thanks to Jessica Murray’s excellent preview, I’ll be heading to the Senate House Library’s new exhibition, which charts the history of housing and poverty in London over the past 200 years – and reveals how much (and how little) has changed. Lucinda Everett, newsletters team

I regularly pace around my neighbourhood (or living room) before bed if I’m yet to hit my 10,000 daily steps. After Kate Lloyd investigated whether this target was arbitrary, I fear I’ll no longer bother. Michael

“Some scientists say that we are living through the largest loss of life since the time of the dinosaurs”: Patrick Greenfield’s piece about quite how much is at stake at the Cop17 biodiversity summit is a sobering and important read. Lucinda

Come Dine With Me fans will appreciate this week’s How we made column on the C4 show. Not sure I’ve seen the episode mentioned where a pet snake crapped all over a dining table, but host-puts-whole-whisk in mouth is a classic. Michael

If you need an easy DIY Halloween costume this year, Guardian writers and readers have got you. Top suggestions include dressing up as a Freudian slip (by wearing a slip dress with “ego”, “id” and “preconscious” written across it) and donning an LED face mask without the light turned on – genuinely chilling. Lucinda
Football | James Maddison scored an excellent first goal, before Omar Marmoush and Ben Davies wrapped up the scoring as Spurs beat a stubborn Coventry 3-1.

Gymnastics | The judge who sentenced the former USA Gymnastics team doctor Larry Nassar to up to 175 years in jail in 2018 for the sexual abuse of more than 250 women and girls has condemned the lack of meaningful change in the decade since Nassar’s crimes were exposed.
Sport | Australian Scott Boland quick ended the day with four wickets against South Africa who finished on 97-5 on the second day of the test match.

“Burnham orders radical rethink of options to fix Thames Water”, is the Guardian’s front page today. The Times leads with “No increase to capital gains tax in the budget”, the Mail writes “Kemi: Budget could be even worse than Reeves bloodbath”, the Telegraph has “Labour cuts £2bn from Army from front line”, and the i Paper runs with “Two-child cap on childcare benefits will be lifted by April”.

The FT leads on “Challenges facing Macron deepen after street clashes reignite French debt rout”, and Metro has “The French correction”. The Express splashes on “NHS is ‘simply not ready’ for another winter crisis”, and the Sun on an RAF crash probe writes “Air heads”.
France protests escalate with riots, looting and 2,400 arrests

Last weekend there were mass protests across France, with more than half a million people estimated to have been involved. The unrest included rioting, looting and violent clashes with outnumbered police in cities including Paris, Marseille and Limoges. The interior minister conceded that police ‘lost control’ in some cities, while President Emmanuel Macron demanded a full security review. Lucy Hough speaks to the Guardian’s Europe correspondent, Jon Henley.
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

In 2022, bird flu wiped out the colony of sandwich terns nesting at Pagham harbour, West Sussex. But their numbers have since bounced back to 756 breeding pairs – and populations of other birds such as ringed plovers and oystercatchers have also increased along the same coastline.

The turnaround is thanks to conservation efforts by RSPB staff and volunteers, which have included removing certain vegetation to make space for shorebirds to nest, and erecting special fencing to keep out predators such as foxes.

The RSPB’s Wez Smith said: “It’s taken several years of dedicated conservation action, but the situation began to ‘tern’ around last year, and the site is now thriving with record breaking populations using it.”

articles.title: Myanmar’s ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi seen in rare photos after receiving gift from King Charles
articles.summary: Critics said images of detained former leader were a stunt by the military to end country’s diplomatic isolation
body: Myanmar has delivered presents from Britain’s ​King Charles to Aung San Suu Kyi, releasing rare photos of the imprisoned former leader in what critics said was a stunt by the country’s military to end diplomatic isolation.

A presidential spokesperson said on social media that home ministry officials handed over two gardening books on soil, “along with one sealed envelope and a sealed diplomatic pouch”, from King Charles, who is known to have an interest in planting and the environment.
Photos showed the Nobel Peace laureate smiling in a wood-panelled room, a paper calendar on the wall behind her.

Suu Kyi, 81, the daughter of the assassinated national independence hero Gen Aung San, has spent much of her life in and out of house arrest for leading pro-democracy movements. She is now serving multiple sentences under house arrest at an undisclosed location in Naypyidaw, the capital.

Over her lifetime, the country’s military rulers have been cautious about locking Suu Kyi away in prison due to her beloved domestic status and international prominence, particularly in Britain, where she lived and married an Oxford academic. Most other political prisoners languish in jail.

Despite winning a 2015 election, she was deposed in a military coup in 2021, triggering an ongoing civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to the independent conflict monitor ACLED. Since then, Suu Kyi’s whereabouts and health have been difficult to determine until an International Committee of the Red Cross visit in August.

Coup leader and former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely condemned as a sham, and has been making efforts to rebuild regional and international diplomatic ties.
Kim Aris, Suu Kyi’s son who lives in London, said in a statement that he welcomed Charles’s gifts but warned their delivery should not be exploited by the regime.

“We must not allow the military regime to use such selective disclosures to create an illusion of normality or gain international legitimacy,” he said. “My mother’s fundamental human rights continue to be violated.”
Min Aung Hlaing remains under US sanctions for human rights abuses, including the 2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of Rohingya Muslims that Washington considers a genocide.
